entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part I.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: January 29, 1990 Tour

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: Interview conducted January 29, 1990 by Bob Zybach and Angela Sondenaa, during a tour of Sulphur Springs and Soap Creek Valley area.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: A.	Sulphur Springs Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're with Charlie Olson at the intersection of Sulphur Springs Road and Lewisburg Road at the base of Lewisburg Saddle. Charlie do you want to tell me where the road that you remember going through here went?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The road was farther over [west], farther over than it is now. And it came across and came out in the road that goes down back of us [Highland Road] and goes past that school house. It came out beyond that school [Crescent Valley High School].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the families that lived there at the school?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was Bessie Murphy's [Gragg] family. Now, when you say over farther you mean on the south side there. It came down the south side of where it is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it left quite a ways back from here. There was a family by the name of Totens over there and then Vineyard, John Vineyard on this side, it took off between those two places and went easterly there and came back where there is a walnut orchard now and it was there years ago, but they haven't grown hardly at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the road as far over at that house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one we see?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, it was quite a ways beyond that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it went beyond that house and went from Totens through Vineyard's and did it go up over Lewisburg Saddle by that route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Will we intersect it up here in a little ways?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We'll be pretty close to it on top. When we go over here, but on the way down we're not in it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would be the next good place to stop from here, would it be up on top?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On top, I think, is the best.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know any houses or any large trees or daffodils or anything of that nature that might be worth stopping and looking at between here and there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And this road, do you remember what year that that was the old route? Do you remember what year it changed to this route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what year they changed things.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could that road have been driven by wagons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That we went then?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Only. Wagons only. There was a turnoff over yonder that went in to another area that . . . I don't remember the different people that owned that in there. There's quite a few names in there that I'm not familiar with any more, but quite a ways over there, there was a gate and another road that went on in to quite an area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the Oak Creek area, that far over?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It didn't go as far as Oak Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you say only wagons could get through, this would be maybe 1900 or 1905, 1910?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wagons would go through, yes, but it was pasture, a whole lot of it was pasture and Sol King's pasture. A lot of that road over there went through Sol King's pasture and there would be let downs of different types of gateways to go through, but wagons was it of course, there was no automobiles yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's a let down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A wire fence with a pole holding the whole together, you know, the different wires, you unhook the loop around the top and you take this whole thing and walk around with it or else you just let it down and drive over it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that an actual road or a right of way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was neither one, and you could go through there and you could go any place really just so you could get through, but there was a let down or some way of getting in from one pasture to another. He had it divided . . . Sol King owned a whole lot of land in here, and he had it fenced off in different blocks so that he could shut the cattle out of one and in another.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But he didn't care if people went through his pasture. Could he have stopped people if he wanted to?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had some kin4 of right of way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was Sol King still alive when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know for sure, when I was little he probably was, but he had a daughter and there's some cabins in Corvallis, I think there's probably eight or nine of them they're right together and they're just alike and this daughter owned all of those cabins and when I got big enough that I could drive around, you know, why it was just common knowledge that she owned all those cabins. I think she was . . . I don't think she was married. I never saw her. I think she was just a single woman.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I have just one more question on that walnut orchard there, did that have a name to it, or just the walnut orchard?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know who owned it. It didn't have any name. But there's walnut. . . there's little walnut trees there yet that ain't much bigger than this. [Shows 4fl6It diameter circle with hands.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything else in this area that. . . how did the vegetation look here, were these hill sides open, can you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. That whole area on the south side here, pert near everything was bare on the south side here. All of these hills in the eariy days were bare. When there was anything at all, it would be oak and then these trees came in and took over and choked the oak out. These trees that are here. You're in the forestry department?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Maybe you can answer some of these questions then. Where did they come from we called them bastard fir when they came in and that wasn't really a beautiful name so it changed to Douglas fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, bastard fir, I think, is woiffir. That's isolated with heavy limbs, it meant there was just a few of them. That's what I've heard so maybe it's changed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were all from the same area it seemed like when they first came in here they took over. We never knew what . . . where they came from, but we called them

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: bastard fir until some where around 19 . . . oh, maybe 1918 or sometime along in there. Why, there were more biblical names, called them Douglas fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when they started calling them old growth for the older trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's . . . that probably didn't start . . the old growth probably didn't start too early, because we called them yellow fir. And that's what they were. They were yellow fir. And my father could bore a hole in one and . . . straight in, and then another one a little higher and then he could make some coals out of oak and put them in one of those holes and with a blower fan them and they would start to burn in there and they'd burn that tree down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's how they removed the trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, no, no, they . . . when they started to really remove the trees was when the sawmills came in. And the railroads would take nothing but that yellow fir. And if there was a round edge . . . just a little bit, just on the sap side, a little round edge on any of one of them they'd throw them out. I worked for Christiansons at the time when they would load out one load after another on that score that they had down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was the Christiansons' fir at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was the christiansons' fir at. . . where you were working?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They . . . little creek, I think, they named it Christiansons after a while. I don't think it was named before. But they had their mill about two miles up on the highway, or three. Up on the highway in Kings Valley, right up this creek and then later on when I started to run school buses in there, why we'd go up that road and then go across over past a gravel . . . manufacturing outfit and they were . . . they called themselves Tn-County Gravel Company.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would that be in the 1930's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was earlier, they were in there earlier than that. And that would come out on Maxfield Creek and then go back down past the church and then to the school house on Maxfield Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On this area here, do you remember when the bastard fir started coming in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Soap Creek over there is where I noticed it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll talk about it there then. These hills were all bare, can you remember what kind of vegetation was on the hills before the oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Native or would people plant grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think it was ever planted. I don't know how it got here but there was oodles and oodles of grass.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Good, yeah. Good pasture for cattle. And it would grow tall because it wasn't pastured down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this would be cattle pasturage, would people run sheep or horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sheep, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Or horses?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not very much. Horses, they had enough horses for their own use just for what ever they needed them for. But there was no . . . that I know of, there was no place where they raised horses for sale or anything like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These hills here, what kinds of wildlife would come in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Gray diggers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Gray diggers. Would there be very many deer in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Quite a lot of deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More than now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. My mother would go out and feed the chickens and she'd called the chickens and the deer would come and eat up the wheat.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the south facing hills at this point though, too, would the deer be in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they were all over.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bear?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not too many. Not too many bear, there were a few panther.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What, cougar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about bobcats?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A few.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you called them panther.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there's a lot of different names for the same animal.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the common name was panther, would people say panther?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what we called them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about beaver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't too many beaver until later. The beavers came in quite a lot later.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when you were young, can you recall any beaver?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Undoubtably there were some but there wasn't many enough to that I noticed them. On Soap Creek they didn't build any dams at the time when I was living up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you ever recall seeing a boomer in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember the location?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Boomer?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where I live now. [Summit, Lincoln County, Oregon]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Not where you live now, this area. Where you live now, there's colonies of them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know of any of them earlier. I had my first contact with boomers was when I moved to Summit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But you don't recall any in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Can you recall anything else about these south hills here, about the types of vegetation that was on it, or the type of animals that were pastured here, or maybe a type of wildlfe that we haven't mentioned. . . coyotes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was coyotes. There were coyotes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about wolves?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was only one wolf that I know of. And that was about 19 . . . I'll have to figure a little bit. When I was aware of it, I didn't know what it was and my uncle came over here about 1910. And I had to go and talk to him one evening coming from school and my sister went on and we went around Bakers Mountain at the time and we went over Bakers Mountain and we went around it the other way. We had three different ways of going to school. And that particular night, why she went home around Bakers Mountain on the north side, or went to the right of it. And

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: when she came to where there was what we called a white house with a big barn, there was something walked out in front of her and it . . . the hair stood up on its neck and it showed its teeth and she didn't crowd it. She just stood still for a while and then it took off. And I had gone over that night, I had gone over to talk to my uncle, to tell him something, he was working for a neighbor and I had my little twenty-two pistol. I wasn't with her. And when I came along he [the wolf] wasn't there. And that was about . . . that same year but quite a little while later, I was alone and I was on the road coming toward the school house and about a mile from the school house something went across the road and it wasn't a coyote. And I went over and talked to Alvie Govier and he had hounds. And he went up there and turned his hounds loose. And they took it. And they never came back. He lost them. So after awhile there was some people named Staits over toward

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Airlie.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Airlie, yeah. And they had some hounds and they got Out of that thing later and they didn't come back. I was working in the [Winney} mill out at Mountain View [Winney's] and there was a fellow that had been up on Soap Creek when I hadn't been there. I'd been gone from there for quite a little while. I can't think of his name now, but he told me that they finally got a timber wolf. He called it a timber wolf. And that apparently was what had killed these dogs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think it was just a single wolf, not a pack or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just a single wolf. How they only got the one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the only one you've heard of in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you ever hear of any white tailed deer in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: White tail?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you mean mule deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. They had white tail in the 1820's, I just wondered if there were any left by 1900.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had two different types of deer here and the white tailed deer is just the most common one, but there was another one that came in and got mixed with these and right now I can't think of what they call that. But it was a heavier deer, shorter

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: legged deer, they never had anything but a spike. They had nothing but a spike, no matter how old they got.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did they come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't tell you that. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then it just inner bred with these deer here? Did they call them something like a "bench leg" or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's it. That's it, "bench leg." That's what it is. Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had bench legs in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they did. They had bench legs here but they were mixed with the others and I shot several of them. I hunted quite a little bit when I was a kid, and I shot several of them. And we were up on the Grass Mountain over in Alsea [River], my wife's father and I and Charlie Rauls. Charlie Rauls had a little shop at that Volvo people are in today in Corvallis. His mother owned that building and he was with me. And it was just about like it is now only thicker, fog, thicker than this and he was down before and we were out in the open but there was bunches of trees in clumps and in rows, different places you know. And I spotted a pretty big deer but I couldn't tell what it was. The fog was too thick and it was only about thirty-five yards from me. And I didn't know where Charlie Rauls was by that time. So I blew my hands a little and then he whistled and he was farther back so I knew he wasn't where he would get hit. And when the fog lifted just a little bit so I could see the outline of this deer again. He was still there. And I shot him. He just went down. I have a little .32- .20 and that's the only thing I use for deer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Still?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Still.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you shoot your last deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did you shoot your last deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I stopped shooting them about twenty years ago, but the last one that I shot was about 8 months ago or six months ago. I can't see with my right eye. I had a little forty a little .44 magnum automatic. And stock is quite short and I figured that if I hold that under my shoulder and then grip that grip real tight and hold the other forearm,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: you know, real tight. And I was squatted down. I had my elbow against my body here and had a really tight grip on the trigger grip and a real tight one on the forearm. But I had bought a box of new ammunition -- that hollow point. And the hollow point was the same size way down deep in there, not just a little cavity And I hadn't shot one of them before. So when I pulled the trigger, that thing came back and the scope caught me right here and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right between the eyes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It tore my nose loose from my forehead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was just six or eight months ago?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About six months ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That wasn't during the season.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I don't think so. I don't remember, it was pretty close to the season, but. . . I started to bleed enough so that I didn't look what happened to the deer. And I just waited a while until it kind of quit bleeding and then I went over to see what happened to him. He'd gone about as far as from here to that white peg right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About twenty feet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And it [the bullet] had entered right where I had figured just back of the shoulder and then it had blew up. That cavity is big enough that when it hits something it would create pressure as it comes back until there is enough air pressure in there that it'll create an explosion and not just a little cavity that will expand and make a bigger hole from there on. Anyway, my wife started to try to make something out of it, and this explosion when it occurred it ruptured the midriff between the chest cavity and the paunch and it ruptured the paunch. And it seemed like it did the same thing with all the rib cage. So the whole rib cage was blood shot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It sounds like you should have been using your .32-. 20.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: B.	Lewisburg Saddle

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we call this the Lewisburg Saddle now, did you call it anything before?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You called it the Lewisburg Saddle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The pass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. I never heard a name for this until the forestry people came through here, you know, and they probably named it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was called no name, the road, would you call it the road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that . . . sure it was a road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just no name to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So if you said you were going to Corvallis, was this the only route through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was the only route except if we went down through the. . . well, we came out through Ed Blake's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's down at the other end of the valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. We could go down that way, but we couldn't. . . at that time the road didn't go where it is now. The road went out at Ed Blake's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we'll go down at that end and then you can show us. Can you remember how it caine up through here, like we can see kind of an old grade down there to our left, is that maybe the way it came up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know just exactly where it went down from here but it went farther to the right here than where it comes up now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so that would be to the west.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: To our right now, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I'm tiying to get things into this [tape recorder] so we can figure it out later.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be towards the ocean or to the west. And it went down to where we were at the bottom of the hill. It came up through Totens; past Sol Kings, through Totens and Vineyard's and then angled back this way, or maybe back over in that way [west] further, can you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We didn't go back that way [west] very far.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We went down here pretty directly down to between . . . a fellow by the name of Toten, and Vineyard was a little farther to the left. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the east?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Towards Corvallis.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you went passed Vineyards.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, we passed Vineyards after we came down to Totens.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. I was thinking of coming up the way we just came but if you're going out you would have gone down to Totens, and then cut past Vineyards and gone out toward the walnuts. And then up here where did the road go toward Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A little farther to the left [west] of where it is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe fifty feet or maybe...

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, it zig zagged.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, but it was off to the left here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was right around the turn of the centuly?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It continued that way until they built this here. I don't know when they built this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall anybody saying when they built this road here, the old road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it called a road or a trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean this forestry . . . [indicates Patterson Road to the west].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. Not the forestry one, the one back when you were a kid. Do you recall when they put that in?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wasn't old enough to know when they put that in, because it was there when I got big enough to know that it was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was this the main route to Corvallis?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people come in by this way to go to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Absolutely, there was no other way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could people take bicycles over it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They could.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember anybody bicycling over this pass here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know anybody that had a bicycle in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. It was possible but they didn't do it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a family that came out . . . they walked from Corvallis and you will have [reference to] him. You've gotten him already on this book. You haven't got him, but you've got his offspring. Moore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the Moores.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They used to live out here didn't they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They would just walk out from.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In the early days, they did live out on Soap Creek. Sam Moore's father lived down there and Sam Moore was probably born there, but his daughters started to come up over here and when they got here they camped right here on top.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so this was a camping area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not normally, but they camped here and they wrote a big sign and tagged it up there. "Snailgate Camping Ground." But of course that was torn down pretty soon. But they camped here and then they went down to Sulphur Springs and camped down there. They came up and visited with us while they was camped there at Sulphur Springs. And we were haying at the time and my father always would read quite a little while after dinner and so we went out and was fooling around outdoors and Iva Moore, Myra was the older one, then there was Iva, and then there was Neva. Neva was the youngest one. But she [Iva] got to talking about . . . oh, they got to talking about getting married and I was just a kid, but I could realize at the time that I was making a safe wager and she wagered with me that she was never going to get married. And it was twenty-five dollars. And I bet that she would get married. She bet that she wouldn't. Now when would she be able to collect?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was pretty safe bet.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. She never could collect it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she ever get married?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But did she remind you about the bet, would she talk about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When could she remind me?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did she remember betting you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we didn't discuss it in later years, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember anything else about this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So can you remember what the vegetation is like right here, was this an open pass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just like it is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just like it is now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So young fir, scattered oak.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't as many of those smaller firs as there is now, but other than the maple, the other brush would be the same as it is now only that the smaller trees that are here now wasn't here then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Were there any old growth trees up here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there were quite a few of them. And there were quite a few others here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: To the east?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be from this area to the east, but now just behind us. . . to the south.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was old growth on the north and it was coming over onto the south side some but there wasn't much on the south side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, could the bastard fir that was coming up on the south side be from the old growth.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it could not have been from the old growth.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why not?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that's a thing I would like to have somebody tell me, what was it and where did they come from.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why couldn't it have come from the old growth [seed] blowing over on the wind or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It wasn't the same thing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, it's a djfferent kind of tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This bastard fir and the old growth was entirely a different type of tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was different?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The bark was different, the needles were different, the wood was different. The wood on this bastard fir won't burn unless it's dry. That old growth -- we'll give it

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: it's right name -- "yellow fir".

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yellow fir, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would burn when it was green. Right at the foot of this hill was one that people had run into in some way with a wagon and they had made a scar and that created a lot of pitch. And they set it afire. And that burned into it a little ways and then went out. Probably somebody else had come along and there was pitch and they'd set it afire. And then it went out. And then I came along afoot. I was about ten years old at the time and I had been to town. I had some teeth filled and I walked and on my way home, I set that thing afire, warmed my fingers a little bit and went on. And my father, I think, went to town the next day. It pert near had to been, he drove in and of course that tree was burned and when he started to come home it was night. He'd always go to the library and read. And he had a horse, just a single horse, and that horse would take him home no matter how dark it was in a buggy. And when he came to that tree, it was down and across the road. He couldn't see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the fire you'd set had toppled the tree?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It had burned just enough so it was down at the time. But he just turned the horse loose, he got in the buggy and turned the horse loose and the horse took him into the brush and went on around and come out on the road down below. About two or three days later, that whole tree had burned up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Completely?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Completely! Completely, and there is a whole lot more back of that that people have never explained. There wasn't enough there but what a fellow could scoop it up and put it in a dust pan and then in a bucket.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think the fires that used to burn through, when they hit that yellow fir could they have burned those trees completely up.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think that may have happened?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It did happen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when they had afire through here, there wasn't a bunch of snags, it was clean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, if a fire could run through without setting them afire because they'd have to develop some pitch in a hole and go in until the fire would be inside of the tree

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: before that tree would start to burn up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But you could burn around that tree with some grass and it wouldn't set it afire. The bark is . . . that's another thing, the bark would be that thick.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About 3 inches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And it would have big clumps on it. You could pert near climb the tree just by getting a hold of some of those clumps. That will never happen to this bastard fir. It's a different species and where did it come from? But, I contend that when you burn wood it blows into where it came from, it doesn't create smog. If you burn something that you have mined out of the earth, it will create smog because it's it wasn't produced from the air. These trees and every other tree . . . every thing that it has gotten . . . has gotten from the air.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are these trees here, do you think they are descended from those yellow fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think these are bastard fir all through here now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course they are.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So what happened to the last of the yellow fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were sold, they were fell and made . . . most of it rail road ties and sold to SP [Southern Pacific] railroad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: fJamesJ Hanish called the older trees the "grandfather trees" and the younger trees the "kids", wouldn't those kids be the descendent of the older trees.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Never.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why not? Where did the younger trees come from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's what I want to know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why didn't the older trees seed in the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw but one place where those yellow fir had a small tree. And that's another question. On the ridge between Wren and the ridge that divided Soap Creek and Kings Valley from there and over towards Wren on the left hand side of that ridge that runs cross ways with these other ridges that run the other direction.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's a cross ways ridge between Wren and Kings Valley and there's another ridge that runs across to the general line of ridges.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Between Soap Creek and Kings Valley there is a ridge [Kings Valley Ridge] that runs cross ways and if you were to get on to that ridge and then take off towards Wren on the left, there was some of those yellow fir and there were some small ones, but the small ones were just as tall as the others. There were only probably a foot through but they were just as tall as the others. And I didn't . . . I'd never seen a small one from a seed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think those trees are still there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They're gone.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, God no, that was . . . I was probably twelve years old when I saw that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall ever seeing any Sugar Pine in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any Ponderosa or other pine. . . natural pine?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just the yellow fir and then the Doug-fir that's in here now that was called bastard fir and then Doug-fir.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's about all that I can think offrom this area. Why don't you finish the stoiy on the bench legs? You'd shot it in the heavy fog and that's the last we got recorded on that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was afraid because it was a spike. But it was so old that some of the teeth were gone. It was a gummer but it was fat, I don't know why. I don't think it would rut, it was right after rutting season, or during rutting season but it hadn't rut. And it was awfully fat, it probably weighed 220 pounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the game warden's name in that area. . . at Alsea?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Clint Haren.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this man you were with, what was his name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Charlie Rauls.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so Charlie Rauls was afraid that Clint Haren would find it and he would get a fine or a ticket.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: an you describe how you got the deer out of there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We put it in Charlie Rauls pick up and we went out through Harlan. He wouldn't go back down through Alsea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You said there was a problem in one of the areas where he was driving the pick up out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, between Burnt Woods and Harlan and on up it's awfully zig-zaggy, an awful lot of crooked road. That's where he hooked on to this piano outfit, I don't remember what they called themselves, but it was a piano outfit and they had a rig that they could move pianos with a pick up, but it was a closed . . . they knew Rauls rig and he knew theirs but he didn't stop.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then you ended up hauling it out that way then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We brought out that way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And those bench legs, you think, inner breed with the other deer in this area and now they're just part of the population.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They've crossed. I've shot several of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Several bench legs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, I've shot several of them that were crossed. And I had one killed after I wasn't shooting here anymore and was feeding them. And it was killed from the road just beyond where this bee man, you know where he's located, over there just north of me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where you live now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Williams. Somebody had shot this bench leg, and it was only a half breed bench leg, but they'd shot it, it was a doe and they had dressed it out but they had left it. They just left it lay there and rot. They'd shot it from the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the bench legs, other than the short legs and the heay chest and that the bucks only have spikes. Was there anything else you could tell was different from the other black-tail deer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were heavier. They were heavier and shorter legged and that was about it. Had nothing but spikes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: C.	Lewisburg Clearcut

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're at the Lewisburg clearcut, at stop 9 on the tour [Soap Creek Valley Auto Tour, Bob Zybach, OSU Research Forests cc: 1989] or stop 10. We're looking out across the south
bracketed_corrections: [Soap Creek Valley Auto Tour, Bob Zybach, OSU Research Forests cc: 1989]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: slopes to the north of us. Can you describe what that looked like?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Coffin Butte of course you can hardly see that. Writsman's Pasture over there, it's pretty near covered, it was bare.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that Writsman's Pasture where we see that patch offir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call that hill up there? Right above Writsman's Pasture, what was that hill called?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I don't know what that was called.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wanda Cook called it Writsman's hill, but you don't remember a name.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It undoubtably could be because that. . . it runs right up through there and Writsman's undoubtably had quite an area of acres. And all of this other here that you can see has got timber on it now, it was bare.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it grass?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Grass and strawberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And strawberries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. That's Bakers Mountain right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's Bakers Mountain off to the left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one that your finger's pointing at is Fogies Mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is what mountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Fogies Mountain. The only name I ever heard for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: F-o-g-i-e?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never saw it spelled but that's .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one with the bald is Fogies and the peak to the right [east] of that is Bakers Mountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one right in front of us is Bakers Mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the lower -- the front profile here -- the vety foreground.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's Bakers Mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay and the one behind it is Fogies Mountain.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one way over there on top of that hill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: With the bald on it. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was Fogies Mountain. And up on there were some big trees that I didn't know just for sure what they were. They looked different from everything else.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Could they have been pine?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No, and I kept wondering for a long time what they were until probably. well, about the time they started to log in there, I found out what they were. They were hemlock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, there was hemlock up in there. Up on the peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've been looking for hemlock all through here. That's why I'm interested in that. Now on Fogles Mountain, that's where the hemlock were.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a heck of a lot of hemlock, old growth, big trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And they logged those out of there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About. . . I could get pretty close to that, they went to Airlie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a mill at Airlie at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a railroad there and that's where they went out. There's a fellow by the name of Winson Reed that bought the old Matthews place up here. That Matthews place joined us on the north and it was 160 acres. And this Winson Reed had his eye on all that timber in there was going to have to come out through there. And he was going to get a little commission on that as it came out, but it didn't turn out that way. They went out toward Airlie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So was that hemlock visible from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that hemlock. . . could you see it from here, from this spot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, sure you could.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, where would it be in relation to that bald?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was where that other green stuff is now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Up along the ridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about down in the draws?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it didn't come down too far. It didn't come down too far until there was fir. Old growth and the bastard fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On these hills here was there any oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Most of the oak would be in the little clumps and they would start I think probably some of it is still visible in places here, I can't tell, but I think they would be oak visible yet there in some places. The oak would start first and then this bastard fir would come right in and grow right with it and choke it out. There would be great big ones about like that, occasionally.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About twenty four inches.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Occasionally. And they would die when the fir trees would come up around they would choke them out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These occasional oak, would they be in small groves or would they be just one or two?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There would be quite a lot of oaks in groves that would come down on these bald places and they would be taken over as soon as . . . it seemed like they have to have fertile ground and moist ground before the seed of these firs would take.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The oak would create a climate for the fir to come in. Did they start growing in the shade of the oak or underneath the branches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Underneath. They'd crowd the oak out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then they'd choke them out and start seeding in the area, and that kind of moved down hill maybe like with the acorn or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they would. They'd come down the hill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How much time would it take to go from the oak to the fir?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, they didn't have any time limit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So some hills would seed in pretty quickly and some would be kind of slow?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It just depended on what the wind would happen to blow and. . . that's kind of an asinine question, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I'm sony for being asinine. On the grasses and the strawberries, can you remember any other kinds of plants that grew in conjunction with those, any kinds of wildflowers or berries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goat weed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Goat weed, is that a native 7

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goat weed took the whole works, all of the bare ground became goat weed and it choked out the strawberries . . . we could go down and pick wild strawberries and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: have a big box and then a bucket, three gallon bucket and then we would have these little buckets that we would pick in and we'd fill the whole works up. Go home and can strawberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wild strawberries?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wild strawberries.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you think the Indians ate them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know whether the Indians. The Indians weren't here yet. Coffin Butte was as far as the Indians had come when I was a kid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What do you mean "had come"? From like the Siletz Reservation?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: West. Coming west. There's a little history that we haven't learned when we went to school. When the white man came here, we started in using the Indians as if they were varmjnts and we started to drive them west. And we continued to do that until they grouped so there was about twelve tribes all together that was fleeing about three days travel ahead of the white man.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You mean right here in the Willamerte Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that was way east of here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, back in Oklahoma or something?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm pretty interested in this Valley right here, now you mentioned that there were artifacts on Coffin Butte.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When they got as far as Coffin Butte, there was a big pit on top and they only way that we could figure it out, the white man could figure it out later, and the only thing I'd heard from it, I never went up there and looked. There was a big pit and they figured that was a place where they tried to stop the white man and hold the white man and keep . . . defend themselves.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that. . the local feeling was that it was a battlement or something, a protective area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. When they left there and came west, why we followed them of course and when we got to Hoskins, they called that Fort Hoskins.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm familiar with the histoty of it, yes.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't a darn sign of any Indians but we built a fort. And of course the Indians fled toward the coast and went north here just like they had done all the way,

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and just like they did when Custer attacked them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that these were Indians that were driven all the way across the United States essentially.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And these were eastern tribes that had been moved into the Willamette Valley by.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Sure, they drove them west and north.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any other people in this area feel that same way, was that considered common knowledge or it that just your theory?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hoskins . . . no, let's see . . . I can't think of that guy's name. At Hoskins, he had a big barn and a good beautiful house

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Chambers.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that wasn't Chambers, there's several Chambers there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Eddy or Norton?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dunn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I knew those too, but then this wasn't them. I can tell you what he was doing, maybe he was representing the British. He was representing the British and he was building a railroad.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hogg or Hoag? Nash, Wallis Nash?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nash. That's the name. He saw when the Indians came through. He saw them come through and they did the same there that they did all the way before. They squaws came ahead.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was watching them, this was in the 1870's or '80's, this is from the Indian Wars, as they were putting people back on the reservation then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why I didn't get it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He saw them when they came through and so he could give us a pretty good description. But he started a railroad and Britain was backing that, but there was another outfit that started and they were also from Britain. And they started to go the other way. And he was trying to get his through first and they were trying to get theirs through first, but they had more money. Now get this, Newport, that was what

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: he was . . . that's what he named that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were in there before Nash. Nash came out here in the 1870's and Portland was 1840's and Newport was 1860's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but we're talking about a railroad to get the produce from the Willamette Valley. And he was trying to get that produce this way to Newport. But they was working to get it the other way, Portland.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: l'mfamiliar with that stoly too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They beat him so, it started to go the other way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back on Coffin Butte, where they had that pit there, you heard local people talk about that pit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I heard there was three pits on Forest Peak. Did you ever hear of those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me which one of those peaks is Forest Peak, or did you know of a Forest Peak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have never heard of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about these ridges and peaks to the right here? Do any of these look familiar?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do they have names?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of. I've hunted all over those. I've carried my little .38-. 55 when I was a kid and I've been all over that area.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did that look like when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was timber. And bare spots.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the bare spots have pretly well filled it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there oak in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: More oak than now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what there is there now, I think it's probably pretty well killed or rotted. My uncle and my brother built a fence. Now we're talking. . . we're going

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: to talk about Ernest Cook.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Ernest Cook, okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And we're also going to talk about Peacock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did Peacock live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They lived just across from the school house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And there was another one, that place that I'm speaking of Peacock, that was the Moore Place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it was Lacy, it was Smith

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that Joseph Smith, John?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know, it could have been an offspring of his, but he had a kid about four years older than me and they got to school they had a daughter, Bessie Smith. My uncle and my brother built a fence, a woven wire fence, with barbed wire around the entire Cook place. That was about eleven . . . I think the Cook place was eleven hundred acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And this other place, Ball . . . Smith, then Dorgan, what ever you want to call it, Moore, that I think was about the same. They built a fence around both of them. Wire fence and they built it with oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that oak off of these hills up through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They cut the oak as close as they could to where they were building the fence.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So they had an eleven hundred acre ranch fenced in there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They got the older oak that was grown in among the fir trees and it was killed, you know, and got dried and was . . . well, a lot of people called black oak because it black. It would turn kind of black after it was dead. And stand, and it was hard.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about Yew wood, did people use yew wood for fences?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That yew wood comes in a little bit on the mountain on this side of the school house of the mountain just to the right, coming home it would be to the right. On there was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: an old fence and it had been some yew wood. Those posts, yew wood posts are setting there when these oak posts are rotten and gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So yew wood was a better post material?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, gosh, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did anybody use the madrone for anything through there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I've never heard of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: it's got another name, they called it something else too. it's kind of a waste wood, it's that wood with the bark that peels off and it's got the leathery leaves to it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Laurel.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They call it laurel too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Laurel, that wouldn't last long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did people use it for anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what it would ever be good for. It was so brittle that you would have to be careful when you fell it, you know, you'd cut an undercut and then you'd start in the back with a cross cut saw awful carefully, if it leaned a little it would be apt to pop anytime and go up a ways and split up there and. . . any direction wherever it would happen to fall. Laurel, I don't think, was good for anything else to but write your initials in. It would never disappear. It sheds it's bark but that initial will be into the next underneath, it sheds it's bark every year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We talked about the animals in this area on the other side. And I want to talk about the fish when we get down below, but can you remember the bird population through here, the owls or the hawks or the pheasant.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a pheasant that we called bush pheasant here, and in Canada they called it fool's hen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Grouse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They called it rough grouse, some of them do, but there's another grouse, a blue grouse, and it's a bigger heavier bird and they are more adapted to the old growth or yellow fir. They are more adapted to that than the owls that they're talking about, because you could find them in that type of timber and I happened to have my little double barreled shotgun and go up through a trail one morning pretty early and there was a lot of fluttering up above and I looked up there and there was grouse, and they

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: were picking buds. And I shot one and it come down, they didn't fly, I shot another

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: one, they didn't fly. I don't know why but they . . . I could shoot. . . I had only thirteen shells with me, I'd already shot two rabbits so when I ran out of shells, I went home. So there used to be a lot of grouse in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they call them anything, did they call them hooters or boorners or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they called them hooters.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember many owls or hawks through this country?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes, quite a lot of them. Quite a lot of them and they . . . they were pretty bad, there was a hawk that was not, not the great big ones, the big ones were bad too. But there was a hawk that was about . . . a little heavier than a pigeon, but they looked a whole lot like a pigeon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're talking about the small hawk that was a little bit bigger than a pigeon.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They would catch the pheasants and they couldn't carry it but they could kill it and eat it. They were probably the worst of the hawks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call them, what kind of hawks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, as far as I know they were no other name.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just hawk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just hawk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the bigger hawks, like the red tails or something? Did you just call them hawks too?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about owls, just call them owls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were hoot owls and then there was other owls, there were small owls, little fellows.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pygmys.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they called them, but they're small. They didn't do any harm, I don't think. They didn't . . . they were probably the size of a robin.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you shoot owls or hawks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I would shoot hawks, yes. I would shoot owls too. Because they were bad, there

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was an owl that got into our chicken house and didn't know how to get out. And it killed several chickens before my mother went over to feed them in the morning and it couldn't get out. There's a little narrow door and it had gone in through that narrow door and the whole front was wire netting and it was trying to get out through that wire netting and she just got a club, you know, and when it would try to get out there why it would stick its head through that wire netting and she'd come down on it with a club. So she had an owl. But they . . . the pheasants

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What you call pheasants are these China pheasants or the grouse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We had no China pheasants yet until . . . they never did come up through the timber up to my place . . . our home. They were down here in this area, there were a lot of them down here and one year it rained so that they couldn't thrash, all the grains was left and the pheasants were awfully thick, they grew awfully thick after that. Down in the valley. Gray diggers, lots of gray diggers.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There's something I've heard of called a brush bunny, in which they said it had short coarse black fur up on the higher elevations, do you recall anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Brush bunny?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a red rabbit that we called a timber rabbit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Timber rabbit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, that's what we called them. And my little shepherd dog would get after one of them and they could go around a while and then if it happened to come back to where she jumped it that's where I would be and I could shoot the darn thing. And if they could get into a log, they would . . usually would, they would get into a hollow log and she'd bark and stay there, and I would come down there and poke it out, you know, and she'd get after it again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were those about the size of a regular bunny or were they more like a jack rabbit?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were not as big as a jack rabbit, but they were much bigger than these little rabbit that we have here now. But they seemed to disappear, but they were good to eat. But the jack rabbit, of course, they wasn't fit to eat. They had warbles all over, you know, I wouldn't want to eat them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you had timber rabbits, gray diggers, do you remember when foxes. . . anything about

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: foxes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was only one group of foxes in this area and that's when Marvin Clark's got away. He had . . . he was raising them for fur.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Red fox?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were not the red, they were the grey, I think they call them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the grey fox was brought in from outside?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. They got away some how and there was foxes for a while, but they didn't last too long, I don't know just what happened to them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. You mentioned pigeons came through this area, was this a pigeon flyway?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The pigeon got to being pretty thick and they . .just down there by Nashville, there's a..

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's the other side of the hill though, I kind of want to keep on this side here. I'mfa,niliar with the pigeons in the Nashville area, just on this side here. Can you recall pigeons from this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah. There was pigeons here. And the only things that I ever was successful with them was with the twenty-two. I had a little twenty-two stephens favorite. And I could kill them with that, but with a shotgun it just seemed like they'd fly away. But they . . . I got a different shotgun and we had strawberries and there was some wild strawberries from the house north and there was kind of a ridge there so I could go down in this side of that ridge with the shotgun and then come on up other and be right on top of them and of course, they'd take off. And this was a pump, and I shot right in to the pile of them and they started to fall and I pumped it and shot again and they started to fall and then they got down by the creek and they lit down there . Mary's River. And they lit down there and every once in a while one would fall out. So they started to move . . . and they went on over towards Summit and Vie Plunket lived in a place where Weavers live now and they got over that fall and they were still dropping once in a while. And I didn't know what Vie was talking about when I met him and he says, "Why don't you take care of your chickens." I didn't know what he meant. And he told me. He told me that those pigeons were falling every once in awhile out of that bunch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The pigeons would fly this far east too? They moved through here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they have chitum or was dogwood, were those major trees at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I planted a bunch of chitum.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I planted a bunch of chitum, I got it from the Arboretum.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's Peavy Arboretum?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. I planted in rows so I could till the two ways. And they. . . pigeons got in there and they . . . teachers in Philomath wanted to come out, you know, and shoot them and they did, and they came out and shot pigeons. I told them they could shoot pigeons anytime they wanted to there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about ducks and geese?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. There was no place much for ducks and geese unless you'd go out to Corvallis and north of Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But in this area here, there was no flyway?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. They'd go over, oh, yeah, they'd go over, but then they wouldn't lite. There was nothing here for them to lite on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: One more thing at this spot here, these trees. . . that they dynamited, do you have any idea why they did that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Why they did it?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't have any idea except if I was to quote Wilson, E. E. Wilson . . . "It probably was Professors that did it."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what E. E. Wilson would say?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You know who E. E. Wilson was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know they named the game farm after him. Did you know him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I should have. My sister was his secretary.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. What kind of man was he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was a nice fellow. He was a real nice chap. She worked for him until she got married and the man she married induced her to go out to the farm where he was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Isee.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And she quit Wilson then. And this man he had a place about three miles south of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Monroe and he was building a house, but he didn't have money to finish it and he didn't have the money to pay for the ranch. And he got her to come out there and he had her pay for the ranch and then he had her pay for finishing the house and she told me "I don't know what he did with his money." She couldn't just sit there, you know, she had to do something, so she got turkeys and raised turkeys. She got a pretty big flock of turkeys and she would take them out to the neighbors where they had grain and they would catch grasshoppers, you know, and eat the grain that was lost and she would transfer them to another place and she was doing pretty well with the turkeys. And then he sold the place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Her husband? When she worked for E. E. Wilson, what was he doing there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was a lawyer.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was lawyer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Why sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why did they name the game ranch after him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Because he owned that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was the land owner.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He owned that. . . well, did you ever see a lawyer that didn't own land.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've seen afew poor lawyers. Not a good lawyer.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he acquired that out there and he set it aside for a game reserve.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, so he created the reserve.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of game was he into?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Chinese pheasants was the main thing. And he planted a bunch of stuff, you know, where they could hide and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So he was creating habitat for them?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now when he would say "it must have been the professors that done it", what kinds of things was he talking about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can quote him. I'll just quote him, that "they're the most ignorant thing that you could ever try to make a contract out for, because they can't understand anything."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he's a lawyer? So when you're saying "it must have been the professors" that blew out these stumps here, you're saying they couldn't quite figure it out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, can you tell us anything about that, that was practical? Can you name a practical thing to take dynamite and blow these things all that high up and then leave them set there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It leads to good discussions.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [ANGELA] The reason they did it was for bird habitat, because a lot of these areas when they go through and they clearcut the whole thing, they don't leave any snags for the owls and the other cavity nesters and the hawks to build their nests in. And so this is something a lot of people are starting to do is leave damaged trees or just old trees and blow the tops out for the birds. Once the forest grows up these will be used --probably every one of them -- for nesting birds of one kind or another. So it's a wildlife habitat project.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that sounds practical for a professor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you're saying that the creation of this kind of habitat for owls, you'd rather see it used for people.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I doubt if there will be a bird nest or an owl's nest in any of those snags.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what's the reason for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They want a nest where they have cover, where it's hidden.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think that these are too far out in the open and by the time the trees come up these will be gone, rotted out or something.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course! They're too open. Stuff won't nest in that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. We'll have to wait another forty or fifty years and we'll check back with you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Those will just rot and fall. [Olson's Note: You'll have to put preservatives in them or they will be down in ten years.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that's interesting on both sides. Can you think of anything else in this area, can you see any places that we haven't maybe mentioned or any types of vegetation that have changed or think of any animals we haven't discussed or types of birds that we haven't discussed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not from this point of view, I don't believe, but farther down we can point out roads where the county roads have been.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Down below I want to get into roads, and houses, and orchards and fish, so we don't want to forget those. I think we covered most of the general patterns of things. And I also want

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: to talk a little bit about your family histoty.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We can speak a little bit of fish here because the whole area is

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This Soap Creek really had good fish and the water was good, you could drink water from any little stream and it was good water and the fish were really good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind offish were they?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Trout.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kind of trout?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you call them brook trout or cutthroats? Just trout?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It could have been both, I don't know. I'm not a fisherman and I don't know much about fish, a little bit about salmon but not trout. I don't know much about them only that I could, without a hook, I could make a hook out of a needle by getting it hot, you know, and bend it. And I could go and catch fish.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How big would the fish get?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, [spreads hands between one and two feet apart].
bracketed_corrections: [spreads hands between one and two feet apart]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Sixteen or eighteen inches?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty good sized ones.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Get some pretty good sized ones?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far up the stream could you get them that big?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's another item, that's another item and it would cover several things that are a little bit extreme but they've got to be. We could go up above our house and go down . . . our house was on the side of the hill, and there was a spring above it and we could get water from that spring through a pipe to the house and we could also pipe if from . . . not pipe it, but ditch it, from where we took water and go down to where we had a garden and irrigate the garden. There was a stream that was far enough up from our house that we could do that you know and it would run. So now rainfall comes in, after a while, and I'm not going to say that it -- falling the timber between here and the coast -- was the only reason for it because I don't know, but that rainfall started to get less and less and less.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Less rainfall now than there was when you were a boy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Less, much less. When I say two hundred inches a year, I'm guessing because I didn't measure it, but it had to be somewhere in that area. And I . . . when I first realized that they was checking it . . . it was pretty close to 100 inches a year. And this is marked at Summit at the Post Office, she checked and 96 was what it was doing when she started and when they moved the Post Office and she moved away I started to keep track and it got down to 56, out in the valley here it was .32. Now there is something there that I have to go back and say that I think it was over 200 inches a year.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would be like Olympic Peninsula or some of the real wet areas up around Valsetz maybe?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what the reason was unless their cutting the timber between here and the coast. But they weren't cutting so much at that time that that could have done it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, like condensation from the trees would be pulling it down maybe, or change in weather patterns, wind patterns.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That will create more when there's a lot of trees, it will condense it you know, and it will fall if there's a lot of timber, but and that later on has proved out but it hasn't been as extreme as that had to be at that time. Now to catch fish if we would go back to where we could catch fish at that time when I was a kid, there isn't any stream.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're going to be heading down to that area, so we can kind of see it from here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You go down to the school house. And there was a little creek that came down from up above and we got our water for the school house out of that little creek. There isn't any creek now. Right below the school house was a bridge across Soap Creek. That bridge floated out three different times while I was a kid and right now I don't think that creek was over it's banks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So you think there's a lot less moisture. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's something else that has changed that I think besides the falling of the trees between here and the coast.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about temperatures, are summer temperatures do you notice much diJerence?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The temperatures vary from year to year and of late years and particularly of this

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: year now, we are having a milder winter than we used to have.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about snow falls and freezes?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Less, it seems like we have less. In 1937, my father started for the barn from the house in the morning and it took him till noon to get over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I talked to Jim Hanish and he said sometime about the mid-30 's there was a three foot snow fall on Berry Creek.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Three foot wasn't any where near to what there was up there. It came up to his neck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would be over five foot.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he would lean and wiggle you know and then he would move forward and my stepmother would come behind and she would tromple it down so that you could walk back and it took him until noon to get over to the barn and it was about a hundred yards from the house to the barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was in 1937?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: 1937. That same year I started to go up, I had a set a snow shoes and I had to take them off and leave them and started in walking and there was a crust on it.
