About three feet up and then it rained and then it froze and that crust would just hold until you were almost on it and then it would break. And it took me about three hours to go from the house and up to the top of the ridge above where Marvin Clark lived and when I got up there, there was a buck laying under some hazel bushes and he saw me, he heard me come and he saw me and when I located him why I just veered off a little bit, you know, so that I wouldn't be going directly at him and went on and I knew that he wasn't going to get up. When it snowed on top of this already. It snowed another two feet and it was on for five weeks and then when it was almost off, why it snowed and stayed two more weeks. Well, I went back up through there and his bones were there all right but he hadn't left, he was still there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was going to be my next question, you kind of anticipated it. What effect did that snow have on the wildlfe population through the area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it almost depleted the deer . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The one bad snowfall knocked the deer population way back.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, it pert near depleted that. They had to. . . I don't know how long it took them to come back. I wasn't shooting very much after that because we stopped eating

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: meat and.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You're a vegetarian?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Oh, no, but there are things that will happen that you have to . . . I like meat and pork was my pet meat and I had to stop it, but

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: For health reasons?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there ever any elk in this area, I've never heard anybody ever mention any elk?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was elk.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right here in Soap Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Until when?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, they were probably out of here by 1910, but I found horns

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Elk horns?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I found a horn that was deep enough covered with fir boughs so that it was a little hard to pick it up and I had a gun that was fairly long and that one horn was as long as my gun. I stuck it up on a limb of a tree and somebody else had found it, I think they took it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jim Hanish mentioned a type of sheep that the early pioneers had might have been wild, it had a curved horn to it. Did you ever find any sheep horns back in these hills? Nothing like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Talking about sheep, on that picture that you have [Soap Creek Schoolhouse student picture, e. 1900), is a guy by the name of Dell Baker. When it had rained real hard, we came home from school and it was just pouring down and my father had just gone up and seen where the sheep and a horse and a dog had come by and had gone on down. And he went on up to see where they had started from and there was a bell strap, cut with a knife and dog tracks and so he followed them down and he came down to where they had been forced across the creek. The creek was a torrent at the time, but there was a foot bridge so you could walk across but he had apparently swum his horse across and he had forced the sheep to go across and he had them up there in his yard and he had about two or three thousand more and . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was two or three thousand sheep in this valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, at that time, yes, oh, yes. But my father's sheep was branded with his special type of brand, an 0 and a bar out from each side, but it was paint. You put paint on it instead of heating the iron. So it was easy to go and pick them out so he had Dell Baker pick them out and bring them back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this area here. . . somehow kind of went from on the south slopes it went from grass to strawberries to oak started coming in and goat weed took over. How did the goat weed get in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know but it grew . . . it grew thick and it just choked pert near everything else out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that during your lfe time or was there goat weed in here when as long as you can remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know of any of it at first, because there was strawberries and the goat weed choked them out you know, and there wouldn't be anything else but goat weed. But it seems to have a cycle. And not only goat weed but silver grays [squirrels] seem to have a cycle. There was a lot of silver grays and I shot a lot of them with my little .22.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would people eat those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, they were good. Yeah, they were very good. And when after a while, they disappeared and they said that seventy-five years they will come back.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are they back?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They did, they came back, there's quite a few out there south of Monroe and in '76 I was building a house over in Alsea, Maitby Creek, and there was three of them there, but people were hunting and they shot them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think they should be allowed to come back possibly?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it doesn't hurt. They've got quite a few at the state house in Salem, but they're not the same, they're either stunted or something. They're not .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They're not the same kind of animal.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: they're not near as big and they haven't got near as much nice fur and the tail isn't near as long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But there used to be a lot of silver grays in this counny?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, gosh yes. Alvie Govier's folks, we were down there to visit them one day and

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: their dog treed something. I went over there, well, it was a big bunch of maples, you know, about four or five trees and I counted seventeen silver grays in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Seventeen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Those were wild, they weren't like the state house, so they used to be thick through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were bigger than those down there at the state house. Prettier. I didn't have my gun. I didn't have my gun with me, so I didn't shoot any of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then it went from this goat weed which you think might be a cyclical thing, might come back choke everything out and maybe go away and then the oak started coming down the hills and the fir started replacing the oak, but on the north side here, this was pretty much the way it is now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was fir there but it hadn't gotten started on the south side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about the draw there then, right along the creek where we're seeing oak and maple and some ash, is that pretty much the same as you recall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there's a whole lot more of this Douglas-fir now than there was then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just along the creek there, though, there's hardly any Douglas-fir along there, how does that compare to the way you remember?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't much of it. There was very little of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: People just pasture right up to the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On this side of the creek, there was quite a bit of it

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On the south side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But on the other side there wasn't hardly any of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So, did the creek run pretty much the same course that it is running now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of any kind of vegetation along the creek like skunk weed or cattails or something that has changed through time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't really know what there is there now. I haven't been up in there and messed around with it. I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. C'an you remember anybody living around this area that we're at right now or anything happening with people in this particular area where we're at right now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can think of something that happened that might be interesting to you. The

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: fellow by the name of William Henry Matthews, and Ernest Cook is involved. He had the place right next to us on this side, 160 acres. And he always wanted to monkey with a pretty foxy horse, you know, and break them but he was old and Ernest Cook discovered a horse that was down here and he had part of the harness on and he got kind of suspicious so he went on up. He knew it was Matthews' horse so he went on up there and he found and traced and checked what had happened. They had started to run away with him, there was two of them . . . they started to run away with him and they had taken him about a mile and there was a place where it was a marshy place and they had put a lot of pole in there tight, close together and when that buggy hit that why it of course bounced. And it probably tipped over and threw him out because he was dead. His head was stuck in the mud and he had it had broke his neck.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was Heniy Matthews, one of the Matthews family in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't any other Matthews that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They called him "Junk" because he used to always had . . . all the houses that he had he filled them full of iron. And they called him Junk Matthews.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But that's how he died with this run away horse?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Isn't there a place here called the Matthews place though, it seems like on the map [Appendix B] that you drew for Soap Creek [School House Foundation], that they had Matthews?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that would have to be up there by Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, let's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was one of them, he had that over from Sulphur Springs, it joined Sulphur Springs territory.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, but he was just a bachelor, I was thinking Matthews family, but Matthews was a single person.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: His family was kind of spread out. His daughters were both gone and married and he married a woman at Falls City named Martin. And they had a boy. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're talking about Aubrey

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Aubrey Martin.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Martin.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he got into the reform school up there. He stole something and they put him in a reform school. And Matthews married his mother and they didn't get along so he moved back over here to where he had these two places here. Aubrey Martin apparently didn't get along with his folks either too good because he came on over here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And lived with Matthews?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And lived with his step father. And his step father of course bought him his clothes and what ever that he could help with why he helped Matthews with it. And I chummed with him quite a little bit.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: With Aubrey Martin?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. He was a nice kid. And now, we'll go back to something that is involved with what you have in here. [Soap Creek Auto Tour Booklet]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: With this guy that has this elephant [tooth]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Glender.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. Glender. We were thrashing right back of that barn . . the water came from that spring where they found this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That down there at the other end of the valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was down there where Glenders lived, out pretty close to Tampico.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you say "Tampico" [tam-PUH-ko], that's how you pronounce it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it wasn't clear down there, but it was pretty close to it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've been to the spring.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Aubrey Martin . . . I will . . . Govier came to me and wondered if I knew where he could find a pitcher and I told him I believe Aubrey Martin would do it, so he went up and saw him, and Aubrey Martin did. He came down and he pitched for them and we thrashed until we were almost through. We thrashed twenty days and we only had about ten more days left and we were thrashing for Glender and the water came from that spring, came down to by the bar with the stand pipe and about an eight foot hose

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and Aubrey Martin came in from the field and took a water bag out from under a wagon and was going to fill it . . . that's the only water they had out in the field you know. And so when he came with that old man Govier was drinking out of that pipe and he thought it would be funny, you know, to turn it on Aubrey when Aubrey came and he did and Aubrey didn't run like he expected him too. He just pulled the cork out of that water bag and it was . . . it probably had two or three or four cups of full of water yet and he just pulled the cork out and run it and shook it over Shorty Govier's head. Everybody laughed you know and Shorty Govier got mad. And he said, "You're canned."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He fired him for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He said, "You're canned, go home. I'll send you your check. I'll mail you your check." And then in the evening he said, "I don't know what we're going to do." He says, "I don't know where we can get another pitcher." I've been a damned fool lots of times in my life and I was then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's what Shorty Govier said?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. That's what I'm saying now. I said, "George," I'll call him George right now, he was sowing sacks with me and I said, "George can go out and pitch and I'll sew the sacks." "Oh," he says, "I'll help you." And he was very pleased about that. And then in the morning we started to thrash and I would get a sack off of there and put it over on a sack pile and come back and he wouldn't have that empty sack on the sacker, you know the other sack. And it run over and I of course had to sow this one and let that one run over for awhile. And when I came back with this . . . after putting this one on the sack pile, why he didn't have this one on. Well, I pushed him away then and put it on. And when you sew sacks a little while and get used to it, it don't take you very long to sew a sack. When you learn how to get the thing up so that you can carry it, it just flies up and hits you. You get your knee under it and you get a hold of the sack on the other side where the ear is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you call them, "ears"?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you call them "ears" on the sacks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We called them a djfferent name when I was a kid, that's what I was wondering.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You get a hold of the one on the other side and your knees under the sack and you're giving it a pull and at the same time you give it a flip with your knee and then you get up off of the two sacks that you're sitting on the sack just hits you right across the chest and you grab it and run. And well, I got him to stay off of there and I made it during the day without problems, in the evening, he would sit down every time at the cook house. You know, he would sit down and figure out what he had made that day. I think it was seven cents a sack for oats and nine, I think, for wheat, I don't remember for sure. But he would Sit down and figure that every night. Then sitting across the table from me and he asked me if I knew how many we threshed that day and I told him, no. And he told me how many. And he wondered if I knew how long it would take a guy to sew a sack. I didn't know. He said, "You sewed two sacks a minute. Bucked, sewed, and jigged." Well, I think I didn't finish what I should have.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were telling the story about the spring and the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This one I didn't finish. If I hadn't been a damned fool when he said, "Where can I get another pitcher?" I should have said, "you'll need two more sack bucks in the morning too." That's what I should have said. But I didn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What's the reason he'd need iwo more sack bucks? What was the reason for that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We should have walked out.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, you should have quit because he did that.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When a man will act like that, you know

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He's not worth working for.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: For a kid, Aubrey was the best pitcher they had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I got you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And when he'll act like that and fly off.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was Shorty Govier that fired him.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did Glender think about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did Glender think about that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Glender didn't give a damn. He was only paying seven cents

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Shorty Govier was in charge of the crew?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Shorty Govier owned the threshing machine.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see, so he was hiring Shorty Govier's threshing machine to work on his farm then.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Shorty Govier threshed for everybody in the neighborhood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I got you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And he had his own threshing crew. And Alvie Govier was his roustabout, that was their younger boy, you know. And he had two sets of horses and there wasn't any automobiles at that time, so those horses, the ones that he used, they went on the run wherever they went. Went out to the mailbox in the morning and got the meat. They had a contract with a butcher to set that out and he'd bring that to the cook shack in time that they could have that by noon. And any other things that they needed why those horses had to go and they got it. They were running all the time wherever they went.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there things that Shorty Govier did later where you said you were a damned fool that you wished you had quit at that time, or just because he did that one thing was the thing.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was all right normally, usually, but that one stunt, you know, that he pulled there. I should have

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Should have called him on it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I should have just told George Benedict. That's the name, I couldn't think of the Benedict. I should have just told Benedict "Let's walk off, let's just walk off." And he would need two more sack bucks. It would have been pretty hard for him to have found them too.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't we go down to the next stop, where I'd like stop now, we're going to start getting into some places where people lived and I would like to get some names associated with them and some roads and trails. Can you remember any roads or trails or anybody living up in this area at all or was this all just timber?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't any here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Just on the road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cook was the only one . . . except us and Matthews.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: D.	Soap Creek Bridge

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we've just crossed over Soap Creek and there's a road now and before there used to be bridge here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There used to be a bridge here and it was quite wide and it would float in the winter time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A floating bridge.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would float [but it wasn't supposed to].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that even when you were a little kid, they had the floating bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So when the water would come up through here and then there'd be a floating bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The water would come up here until you couldn't cross.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who built it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who built the bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any family living through here or anything like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, no families lived here. But Matthews had this forty acres up here above Sulphur Springs.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Let's go on to Sulphur Springs from here.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: E.	County Road Oak

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're looking. . . these fir trees around the oak weren't here, and just the oak were here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the only thing here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No other trees?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No other trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what did the county road do at this point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The county road went just beyond that. It stopped probably where that mailbox is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, this was the end of the county road, right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was the end of the county road right here. There was a barn right in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, off to the left of the mailbox was a barn?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About how far off?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, just far out enough so that you'd miss it when you drive up here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the barn. . . whose barn was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We have no idea.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was an old barn when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there was an old barn here about 1900, it was real old then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this was the end of the counry road at this point?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [ANGELA] Was the barn on this side of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Maybe 50 or 100 feet from us?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right at the edge of the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, right at the edge of the road. Maybe on this little flat here we can see? Maybe by that state refuge sign? That yellow sign, can you see that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty close to there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so was there a circular turn at the end of the county road around this oak here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, you couldn't drive around it, but it was open on the other side. It was on this side of that oak.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so this was a landmark kind of, this marked the end of the road. Did the oak have a name, or did this road have a name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just the county road, I don't know of any name. They didn't have them named in those days.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, all these roads beyond this point here are. . . were private roads?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was that barn used for anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was all open in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This whole area down here to Sulphur Springs?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That whole area was open, it was just a big open area, and campers would come in

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: here. Tents, put up tents, and up in right in there somewhere was a hotel.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's. . . I'm interested in finding out about that. But from this point here, how long was that barn there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: How long did it stay there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I have no idea when they tore it down and when it disappeared because I wasn't here at the time when that happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it was after you left?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that barn was there for twenty or thirty years, did people camp out in it or. . . use it for anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Originally, apparently somebody had used it. They didn't use it when I knew anything about it. It was too old then. And this hotel up here was old then. And this had been a camp ground, they'd bring their own tents up here when they camped here. And I don't know if I told you about that big tree that they had . . . that they had cut up from both sides of the creek. There was big tree just a little ways from this hotel. They had cut it up for wood on that far side of the creek and they had cut it up for wood on this side. But it set right across the creek there and it was rotten, when I was a kid it was rotten. But walking across that widened it on top, you know, so it was easy to walk across. One night during the night there was a big noise and a guy got up and took a 30-30 with him and went out and there was something big over there and it was dark and he couldn't tell what it was. And he took a shot at it. And it didn't move so he went back in. I don't know if he came out of the hotel or if he came out of a tent because I didn't see this, but I . . . the people told about it you know. In the morning, they found that the log had broke and fell in the creek and this chunk of it was setting up there on that side and he had just seen that chunk, it was dark, and he just aimed and shot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was before you were born maybe, that that happened? it was an old story?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It happened while I was here. While I lived here. That happened while I was right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We lived right across the hill here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and this is the area we want to try to get familiar where the houses were and what people did and look at the places where people lived like the Bakers and your family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Bakers didn't live up here and my family didn't either. Bakers lived down there right across from where Cooks lived. And we lived over on the other side of this ridge. We could see the mountains there, but you can't see it here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we'd go in from maybe another road?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The county road that stopped here . . . this is something that the people wouldn't be able to find right now. The county road was on the other side over here, it flipped. And it came over to the ridge here and it went right up the ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right up this ridge to our right here was the old county road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It went right up that ridge, and up through where it hit our home and it went through our home and went down on the other side to Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Kings Valley is just up and over. . . and that road isn't there anymore?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it's pretty hard to find it. I don't know whether I could find it all along but I know I can find it in places because where the road would be and the wheel tracks wagon wheel tracks, the seed, the fir seed, there would be nothing but stumps now but there were trees then of course, they'd start right in the wheel rut and we can find it probably by seeing where there'd be a bunch of wheel tracks with stumps probably about that far apart and straight. But there'd be no need of going up there because it goes right up the ridge and goes through our 160 acres of ground and goes out on the other side where it's called the Longfellow place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, let me write that down, I haven't heard of Longfellows before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And down to Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, at this end here then, while we're on this spur, I wasn't sure how these roads went, but we can go up here to Sulphur Springs, maybe get a drink of water and kind of look around here and then start back down the other road system there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any orchards or any other trees other than this one to our left in this area here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No orchard, but if you talk about trees there's a whole lot of yew trees and they're still there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm familiar with this area, so. . . but I'm thinking of trees that people used. Like they used this tree here as a landmark. Or they used. . . did this tree have a name or just the oak tree at the end of the county road, something like that? Do you recall any name associated with this tree, they name it afier anybody or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, hell, they didn't name . . . every tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I know, but sometimes they would. . . there'd be a tree at the end of the road and they'd call it the "hanging tree" or "Smith's tree" or something like that. Nothing, just this tree just happened to be here, kind of a landmark.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The only thing that I know of was that there was a tree there and it was the end of the road. I've never hear anybody name it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: F.	Sulphur Springs

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at Sulphur Springs and you were telling me the hotel was down there to the right, and right in front of that brush that we can see. And this whole area, this whole side here didn't have any trees or anything in those days.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was open.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What kinds of plants grew in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Plants'i

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Like grass, strawberries, or goat weed.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had that trimmed up pretty good in there. There was tents . . . there was a lot of tents in here, they camped in here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would the tents kind of be in this open area that's here now?. Is this kind of where they put the tents?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Of course.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would anybody camp on the other side of the creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was nothing on the other side of the creek but trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you say there was a trail that went over to Oak Creek from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This trail goes right through here to Oak Creek and old Junk Matthews took a notice

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that he was going to make a road through there one time. He started it. It's only four miles . . . about five miles.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From here to Oak Creek?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where did Junk Matthews live from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right up there just about as far as you can see a little bit farther beyond what you can see, was his forty acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where was his house at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just about the middle of the forty acres.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would be quite. . . so there was. . . was he the only family up this little stretch here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the only family here at that time, but there is something else. Missed a kind of little detail, years ago they had put in a sawmill up here and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you find that spot?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Water power.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A water power sawmill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Water power sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you find that spot, I'm real interested in that? Can you find the spot where the sawmill was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I doubt it, because there's trees there . . . I don't know how many families live up there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't know either, we've got a key to the gate. Why don't we talk about Sulphur Springs right here and then take a little drive up there to where Junk Matthews' house was and you can just point out generally where the sawmill was, does that sound all right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think I can point out pretty closely where it was, but there's . . . his house I can point out pretty close where it was, but I don't know what they've got up there now. There's undoubtably a bunch of houses up there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't know either so we can find out together. How about this hill up on this side here [north], what was this like over here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was bald.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: All of it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was bald.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this road that's going through here now this rock road. . . was there a road going. is this Matthews' road here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a sort of a trail that you could drive up there with a buggy or a horse, but that was all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About where the road is now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Families camped out here what would they do?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't check on them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've heard of a croquet field here, can you remember a croquet field ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they play the game called croquet? A woman a little bit older than you said there was a croquet yard in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Not that I know of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were there any tables?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. They put tables in here when Roosevelt was President, yes, they put some tables in here then, yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The CCC'S?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And the Ccc's were the ones that put that rock down there as near as you can remember? That concrete slab?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, they did, they put that on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So people would come in from town about where the oak tree is and they'd set up camp here. How long would they camp, how long would they stay?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think they had any fixed time. And of the dozens that come in here, how the hell would you expect me to answer that question.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just of the top of your head. Would anybody camp out over here on this side of the trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they all stay in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were in that camp ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why would they come here instead of someplace else?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't ask them. This up here was bare and there were gray diggers up here. I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: could shoot gray diggers from here with my father's .45-.75. Lots of fun to shoot

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: gray diggers up there. Off on the left you said, there was a fenced off area that. . . was that at the same time that people camped. You said, a man was breaking a horse in here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was where they camped yes, when they came out here and camped, they camped on the camp grounds.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the fenced off area, would people put their horses in there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know if it . . . I never saw a horse out here except when he. . . Dell Baker owned.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did the Bakers own this piece of ground right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They did, they owned this piece of ground.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they charge people rent for camping, or was there any charge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He just.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In those days, the people were not as greedy in those days as they are now. I don't think they charged for it. I never heard of them charging anything for it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On that hotel that was a two story hotel, do you remember about the dimensions of the hotel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I could tell you pretty close to the dimensions all right but it was probably forty by forty. It was a pretty good sized building, it was a well built building.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you hear any stories about it? People, did they call it the hotel or Sulphur Springs Hotel?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they called it but there were stones to the regards to this, like there was down at Tampico. That was really a liquor outfit you know in there and crime.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Crime in Tampico?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was four brothers, Lee Brown was one of them, but Lee Brown was the only one of them that hadn't murdered somebody.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In Tampico, what years was that about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what year that was about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the Browns were the four brothers, and three of them had murdered people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Lee Brown was about fifty years old when I worked for him and I was about

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: fourteen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he had three brothers that had all murdered people?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. One of them . . . one of their names was Clint, and he had one of these little single stage race . . . two wheeled rigs you know that they used to run races with with just one horse. And he would come up here every week all winter. summer, not winter, he'd come up here and drink this Sulphur water.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just for his health?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So people might have been coming here to camp out for health, like a.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was why people were here. Now did they call that area down there Tampico when you were young, did they still call that Tampico in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. That was still called Tampico and I think it still is, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, and then. . . it was known as a. . . you say, a liquor outfit. Did they have the tavern, was that still open when you were young?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they had there. I didn't go down there when I was a kid.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It had a bad reputation when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you name some of the people that lived in the Tampico area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, of the later ones, you know, I could. Will Glender was pretty close to it, you know. And Charlie Glender was pretty close to it and there was a. . . I thought of his name this morning, trying to think of it right now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A turkey farmer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know. I'll probably . . . I can think of that probably after I stop trying.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you remember any special stories from Tampico, do you remember any particular stories? Mostly, it was a bad place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I didn't know of any stories that were bad only that I knew it was a bad place because people talked about it, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember any stories about black people or Indians in that area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know of any indian artifacts that might have been found in this area, any arrowheads

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: An occasional arrowhead could be found almost anywhere in here and on my place where I live today, I have found some.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On this area here, the hotel was there and did you. . . do you want to talk about it burning down or about what year it burned down or any circumstances concerning that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, I could come pretty close to the year when it burned down, but the circumstances I can name the guy that burned it, but I won't do it. Because he had two . . . he has two daughters now that tend to . . . they're a part of our [Soap CreekJ school house foundation.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see. Do you know the reason why he burned it down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Spite.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was somebody living here at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Aubrey Martin.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, Aubrey Martin. . . the person you were talking about earlier was living at the hotel.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was living here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He used that for his home.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it still Baker's property at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I kind of believe that it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Aubrey Martin was living on Baker's place and then he had problems with somebody else who burned his home down.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I think probably . . . I know the old Tom Baker was dead and I think that Dell Baker was dead and did you ever hear about this Youngblood, coroner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He married Mabel Baker. I can't think of his first name, but Youngblood. They were just about one of the first coroners there in Corvallis.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [CHARLIE OLSON ASKED US TO STOP RECORDER AND THEN RELATES STORY REGARDING THE BURNING OF AUBREY MARTIN'S HOME] So he. . . was Aubrey Martin living here by himself?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, Matthews would bring in people here that he figured would settle. And he brought two families in here, I can't remember the name of this one, but Schneider

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: was the name of the other family. He brought them both in here at the same time. This Schneider family had . . . there was a boy and a girl and then their mother, and the father left them. These other didn't have a family. And he left his woman. And they .. I don't know anything about their circumstances but Aubrey Martin was living with this other woman, here, in this hotel.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And no children, there were no children?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. But on this other situation, Schneider, there was a fellow from Corvallis that would come out here, you know, and stay with them and Gene Schneider, he was about eighteen, he got tired of that and he said, "you've got to let that guy go or I'm going to leave". And that gives you a pretty good idea why their husbands had left. And this Mrs. Schneider says you can leave. Gene Schneider worked for Cook, Wanda would probably know him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, Gene Schneider.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was clearing land on this side of Cook's house. He was clearing land down there and that was the only income that they had. And so you can't blame him for wanting his mother to let this guy go back to Corvallis where he belonged. He shouldn't come out here and live with them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But the mother told him he could go. And he went. And he joined the Merchant Marines. And the last that they heard of him, that ship was sunk and he was a pretty good swimmer, but he was on a couple of planks, whatever happened from then on they didn't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Never heard from him again?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to Aubrey Martin after his house burned down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he was around for quite a while but I don't know really what happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to the woman that he was living with?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so. . . Junk Matthews got killed a few years later on the horses like we've already said. Did anybody live beyond Junk Matthews place, was this the furthest place out in this area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: His place was the only one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But where did Schneiders live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the other side of this ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so they were up on another road system?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They went. . . they lived on the road that goes up to where I lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now in this area here then, we had a two-story hotel, there used to be benches around the spring and it had a concrete fountain. can you describe that fountain?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was pitcher like, of cement.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just like a cylinder?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was round, I'll tell you how they put it in, they started to dig for it and the stuff would keep running in, keep running in, they couldn't dig down for the thing, so they got on it and worked it down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, just a bunch of people pushing it in to place. So was it like a standard fountain like you could buy for at a concrete place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You have seen a pitcher pump?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, it was a pitcher pump.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You have seen a pitcher pump?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, this was a cement rig built like a pitcher pump, the spout came out just like on a pitcher pump.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I see, so it came up and over. Did the spring have any more pressure in those days? You say a stronger flavor.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was stronger than it is now. There's nothing to it now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We thought there was something to it. I drink it every time but I never tried to gulp it before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, maybe my taster isn't as good as it should be, but.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were the benches that were built. . . built around there kind of rough benches or were they kind of elaborate?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were wood, one on each side.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were they permanently put in place or could you move them around?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were permanent.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What were they set in, were they stakes in the ground, built on that or..

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a floor, there was a floor in there and they set on the floor.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there a roof or any side walls?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the floor, was it a wooden floor?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So plank? So this was pretty well, built up right around that spring then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was a wooden floor, tongue and groove.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And it had an open field and people would have tents, a house that people lived in sometimes, or the hotel, was it ever vacant? Or was somebody always living there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dell Baker lived with his folks down here just on the other side of where Cooks lived.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any garden or orchards here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you think of anything? I think we have a clear picture and I think we've covered. can you think of anything about this area here that we may not have mentioned.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can think of something in regards to that power for that sawmill.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's go up that way next here.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: G.	Junk Matthews' House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We are up here by a red house, and we're on probably the south east corner, we're just entering what looks like a horse ranch or something here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I wouldn't have any idea what they've got here now. The house, Matthews' house was right in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About maybe where that barn is or where the fences are down there or horse trailer?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't tell what that is down there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it would be off to the lower left of us. What kind of house was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just an ordinary wooden house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall any orchard or anything in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nothing.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the saw,nill have been from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The sawmill was up there quite a little ways farther.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But they had a flume they caught water and they trapped it and they had built what you could call a silo today. They had built it with two by sixes laid flat clear around, not edge ways, but flat ways in order to make sure it was strong. And they had built that up until I don't know how many thousand gallons it could hold but it was pretty big and it was up on a stand so that there would be quite a little bit of pressure when they would let that water come out of there. And they would drain that on to a paddle wheel. That was their power and they would saw and then of course when they ran out of water they would stop sawing and then they'd go ahead and fill that up again and when it was full why they would saw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you find approximately the spot where that sawmill was if we drive up that way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Approximately maybe, but I can't tell you I can find it because everything is different now, you know, I don't think that should make such a hell of a lot of difference.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The reason it makes some difference is that was probably the earliest sawmill in this area, or one of them and if we can get the approximate location they can excavate below ground level and some of the anthropology classes they have now, it would be an interesting school project or an interesting research or education to teach people how to do that, so if they can locate it, and they've done the type of research we're doing today, trying to reconstruct things the way they were.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can make a guess at approximately where it set.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why don't we drive up there and take a shot at it.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: H.	Sulphur Springs Sawmill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're up between a cyclone fence and a new logging road to the left and we're about 100 or 150 yards before the gate. Can you kind of point out roughly where you think the sawmill may have been?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Where?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Approximately where?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, we're pretty close to where it was right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, would they have a log yard out in here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A log yard, did they deck the logs in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They pulled the logs down with oxen.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, with oxen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They pulled them down here with oxen, and they had a skid road up in there and when I was in the school bus business, I went up to the . . . darn it, they had a law suit, court house, I went to the court house but I had a schedule, you know, I had to leave right . . . I couldn't stay and see when it was over. There was a lawyer in Portland, Gitner, he was trying to tell them that this road here had been a highway, county road, and I sat in there awhile and listened and then I had to go on my run. So I couldn't tell just what they had, but anyway this whole hillside was bare. These little trees here now were not there. And Lee Brown, I mentioned him, Lee Brown was on the witness stand and they were trying to get him to say that this had been a county road up through here. So that Gitner owning land and timber up above here could get that road up through there so he could come out through here and that they would keep it up because it was a county road. That was what he was trying to do. I had to leave but Lee Brown was on the witness stand and he said, "I have rode my horse all over that area chasing cattle," and I don't know what he testified later because I had to leave. But this guy Gitner later on, Cook wrote me a letter and warned me of Gitner. He had . . . he had had some trouble with him, because Cook owned this other land in here, you know, and Gitner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was Matthews' land and C'ook's land went out from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, Cook's land went beyond here, we've seen where his land was, you know, my uncle and my brother built a fence around .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That area we could see from up there fat Lewisburg GlearcurJ.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But Gitner had tried to steal something from him, and he wrote me a letter and told me to watch out for Gitner.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: On Matthews' land, was this sawmill on Matthews' land?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so beyond Matthews' land, who owned that land out there, before Gitner?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what Gitner did, that was probably state, there was quite a lot of

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: government land yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Public domain.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, there was quite a lot of that yet in here and also S.P.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Southern Pacific.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: owned a lot of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From the old 0 and C lands.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this area here . . . was the sawmill called Matthews' sawmill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what they called it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when it operated?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I wasn't born yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was before 1900?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, do you know of any other sawmill that operated in the Soap Creek Valley before 1900?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this one here, was the water wheel, it was still in existence, you saw that when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they had taken it Out when I saw it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You've just been told about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I saw the tank, and I saw the flume and I saw the skid row where they had hauled the logs down with oxen. That's all that I could see.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the skid road planked?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just a regular skid road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a regular skid road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Which way did the skid road go?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It went up into the timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Pretty much along the line of this road now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right in the valley, right in the draw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, how about the flume, do you know what happened to that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was gone before I was big enough to come over here and look, I never saw it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what kind of saw they would have been cutting the timber up with in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What kind of what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Saw? What kind of saw? Circular? Reciprocal?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The saw, circular saw was the only thing they knew of at that time. They didn't have a band saw yet for years. And that became quite a thing later on, you know, band saws came in.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would they have been cutting up yellow fir, do you think, would that have been the product?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They cut the yellow fir, yes, that's the only thing they had to cut here at the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This bare area here, we're at pretty much the end of the bare area; did it start turning into timber by the gate there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you wouldn't have to go very far beyond what you can see here until it was pretty much timber.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that would go clear to Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Timber all the way to Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No openings or anything like that? All the opening were pretty much here in Soap Creek until you got to Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These little . . . all of these little oak trees here have come since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This was all bare.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is kind of where the bare area ended and after this it was timber?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then, could you get to Kings Valley by going this route?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You had to go back over.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You could get there all right but you'd go through an awful lot of brush.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so how would you get to Kings Valley from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, you'd go up the other creek. Go up the other creek and go up that other road. where there was a county road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we've got the sawmill here, we've got Matthews' house behind us, did Matthews have any barns or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He didn't have any barns here at this place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we would have had a sawmill, we would have had Matthews' house, would have had the old hotel, and then we would have had the barn right by the oak tree and that would have been the only structures through this area that you can remember.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That barn over there that we spoke on, there was a wagon, a buggy in there when I was big enough to run around. There was still a buggy in there. And we took it out and Elmer Govier was with us when we did that, and he was probably one of the big guys at the head of that. We took it out . . . there was some people in Corvallis, this isn't . . . this has nothing to do with it, but there was some people in Corvallis that was up here at the Springs, Sulphur Springs. And we thought it would be a joke to take that wagon out and put it in the road and take the wheels off of it. And we did that and then we went back on down. And they stopped at Govier's house when they went back out and asked old man Govier, Elmer run and hid when he saw them coming. And they asked the old man if Elmer Govier was around. And Elmer had told him, "Don't tell them I'm here."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Elmer Govier sounds kind of like a trouble maker a little bit. One last question on the /zotel, do you have any idea when that was built or when it shut down?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, when it was burned up, I can tell you pretty close, when it burned down, it would be pretty close to the '30's.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it shut down. . . did people rent rooms out by 1900?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was used at all by the time that this . . . this had faded out, people had automobiles when that thing burned down and there was quite a lot of stuff went every where else, you know, but they didn't come here because this was . . . this was kind of an out of the way place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this was pretty popular before 1900.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then it kind offaded out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it was still pretty popular when I was big enough to run a foot race, so

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Until 1905 or 1910. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, 1913 was when that was

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Just up about until World War I, or up till the automobiles, right up until then it was a popular place to come.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was just about 1913, that they had a foot race on that. . . and I entered it. And Otto Han, do you know him?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, I sure don't.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: South of Corvallis. Well, he was here, but I didn't know him then. I got acquainted with him later on. And I had four miles to school and it was steep and it was regular. In those days they didn't have kids to exercise, you know, at all. And I had a heck of an advantage. And I could run away from anything that they'd stick out there. And I run a foot race here and they had a guy that was going to run with the winner. And I made an ass out of him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, did you get anything for winning the foot race?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How far did you have to run?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: One hundred yards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was a sprint.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it an organized thing or was it just kind of an informal competition?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was just something that come up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Another one came up just north of Corvallis about a year later. Otto Han was there and I didn't know it. I ran that one, but that one I had a disadvantage. We had button shoes in those days, and the last couple out, and they had hauled wood out of this area with wagons and then of course the wagon would make a track about that deep and about that wide. And they had mowed it and left the grass on there and I sprained my ankle. Otto Han was there. I knew he was there then because he had a sister there, I don't remember her name now, I had just met her that day, but she was pretty athletic and I got her for a partner and nobody would catch us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you with the sprained ankle too.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, not yet, not yet, but I sprained it there. Button shoes was the thing then, and I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: put strings in the hole and so I would button it over the string. And got over, there was a rail fence you know in the shade and I sat down and watched the rest of it. And my brother came up and he said, "You've got to get over here and sign up, they're signing up for races" and I said, "With an anide like that," and he said, "Yeah." He says, "That won't brother you." And I said, "I can't run with that." And he says, "You can win it on one foot." Well, I had quite a lot of faith in him, he was ten years older than I was. And he kept on, and I finally got up and went over there and we started to sign up and I was going to sign up with the boys, you know, and he said, "No, you sign with the men." Oh, God, no. But he insisted and I did, I signed up with the men. Well, they had a little cap gun and that went off, why of course I just gritted my teeth and I used it just as if I hadn't sprained it and took off. And there wasn't anything too close, I didn't look around but I could hear them. And when I got to about thirty feet from the string why of course I put on a little extra and took the string. I didn't realize that Otto Han had been up here, I didn't know him at that time. But I had a big advantage over everybody. I could out run anybody that could stick at me, you know, at that time because going to school starting at six and continuing until I completed ninth grade, I told you about Miss Allen, she taught the first year of high school here, and that was the thing, you know, morning and night, evening and morning and four miles and hilly and then after coming home, probably that much more, I had to chase the cows home. I sprained it another night.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about that race there though, what happened on that one, you were thirty yards from the string?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Huh?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were up thirty yards from the string and you started to give another burst, did you win that race too in 1914?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: With the sprained ankle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah, that didn't bother me at all.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This Otto Han could remember that? He told you later about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You must have made an impression on him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he didn't realize the advantage that I had.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: From all that exercise.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And I didn't either, but you know, they didn't have anything in the way of athletics in schools in those days. But I learned something in the later years that I was chasing cows to try and get them home. I had a little shepherd dog and I was . . . I got them started and they went around me and headed on the road to Kings Valley, I told you about that county road that went right through.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We want to go over there, too, before we. . . try to beat some daylight.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was trying to get around them by running in the brush and it was getting dark and there was a big log. I got up on that and jumped and they were just about even with me, I could hear the bells and I was almost ahead of them and when I lit on the other side, something turned my ankle. That time I really turned it. So, I hurt it, . . . it made me sick, you know, I just in desperation and anger, I said, "Sic'em." And my little dog left. And the bells began a ringing a little harder and a little harder and a little harder and pretty quick I began to realize they were coming closer and she had gone around them and they were coming back. And they started for home. They were going just all they could go, you know. And she came back for me after while and I found something that I could use for a crutch and I started for home. And when I got to where there was a lot of openings on that Longfellow place up above our home and on the Kings Valley side, I heard one clink of a bell. Over on the other side was a few open areas and they had a trail through a bunch of small trees and I got onto that trail and started to go over that direction and after a while I could smell cattle sweating and I knew I was right among them and I just said, "Sic'em." And she took them. Well, I didn't get home as quick as they did. But when I came home they were in the barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Smart dog.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I learned then, but it was pretty late in the game, I learned then when those cows was going to go home, just tell them "Sic 'em." That little dog would take them. She'd grab them right by the hock, you know, and then duck back and they would strike at her but she would be back and too low and before they could get anywhere why she

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: would have them by the other hock.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was the dog's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Trixie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Trixie, okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: I.	Soap Creek Road

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, we just passed the bridge, the first bridge on the left coming from Sulphur Springs and you said Joe Hansen built that bridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but this has been rebuilt since.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember when Joe Hanson built the bridge though?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have been pretty close to 1940.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1940, okay. And there was a house where we just passed the bridge and we're looking on the right here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no house here at all at that time. There was no house here at all, but the county road came out right back yonder.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where that trailer house is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it came out right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it crossed this creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This one on our left here now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It crossed this creek some where right here, it forded, there was no bridge across it. There is now here, but .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There was a ford here, so this. . . we've got an area right down there, Angela can probably see it off to the left and we've got a slope down here in these alder here that looks like a slope to the bank. Yeah, see that right off on our left here could that have been the ford?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't see, I'll have to turn around.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's kind of subtle.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no trees in there at that time, but there's where the county road crossed and . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is the old county road. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And it got over to the middle of this ridge that goes up here . . . that we saw to our

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: right when we were stopped up yonder.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that's now on our left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It went over here and then went right up that ridge. And it stayed on that ridge until it got up to our place and then it went into our place and went through it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So let's. . . we can't get up there today, so let's say we're on this county road and we're heading west across the ford in this creek. Does this creek have a name here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. It was just part of Soap Creek.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did any body live down in this area where.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nobody, there was nobody here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He [Cook] would have had to have owned this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so we're at the Cook's place right here, [with the] county road going down the valley, it's crossing on this ford here and this is just kind of open field here then. There's nobody here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was nobody living . . . we were four miles from our nearest neighbors.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So then coming up towards this ridge here, did the road cut sharp to the right or did it just kind of angle up the ridge?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It just angled up that ridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So maybe it intersected it maybe over there about ten o'clock or something like that? I might be able to find that on the ground, so. . . it went up the ridge and how far up the ridge was your place?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That county road stayed on the ridge until it came up to our place and it still stayed on the ridge and went through our place. And went over on what was known as the Longfellow place at that time. And the Longfellow place. . . had some prairies that we called Fern Prairies, there was no trees on it, and it went through there and right down a canyon to Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this ridge line goes all the way through to Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the county road that went right through to Kings Valley.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Because I think that road's been in there since the 1850's. I think they hauled lumber over that in 1850. That's why I'm real curious about U. Were there an orchards between this point here and your house?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [ANGELA] [exasperated] Nobody lived here, Bob. They could have had pioneers that lived here before. . . or they could have planted orchards

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: people, most people planted orchards right around their houses, didn't they? They'd be apt to live there, there would have to be a place there at that time, but there wasn't. Right here there could have been a place, because there was some roses right about . . . just a little behind where these cars are was a bunch of roses and some bricks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay. And where these cars are, right in front of the Ponderosa pine there, looks like Ponderosa, something like that. There was roses and bricks right in that location and that was. . . was there when you were a kid. Were there any apple trees around here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How about up on your place? Did you have apples up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: My father planted some Bismarks and some Baidwins and two or three others, and a sweet apple, and a Royal Ann cherry tree, and a Black Republican cherry tree, and pie cherry tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know about what year he planted those?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he built that house when I was newly born in the log cabin right down below it. And he planted those trees soon after he got that house built, he planted those trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So right around the turn of the centuty, right around 1900.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It probably would have been 1901 or 1902 when he planted the trees.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Are any of those trees still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They were the last time I was up there, they were there, but there was stuff growing all around them. He made. . . here's something on this wood again, he made that roof out of this yellow fir, he split shingles, he made shakes out of that and sold shakes to anybody that would want shakes. He would burn the trees down, I told you about that, and when they would fall, he would saw them off, you know, so they wouldn't go on up and burn up completely and then he would make shakes and he would sell those shakes, but when he built that house, he made shingles and he shaved the shingles with a draw shave and those shingles were on that house about ten years ago.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that house still there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, they were starting to leak and when they started to leak, why of course the water went down and went through the floor and the foundation began to give way and the last time I that I was up there, the house was almost down. It had started to fall down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was the last time you were up there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: About fifteen years ago [1975].

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long would it take to walk up there from here? Not today of course, but.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think I would want to tackle that, I'd go up the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This road here goes all the way up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This road does?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yes. But you're going to run into something when you get over to this Matthews place. When you get into that Matthews place, he had built a house right on a pinnacle and it was pretty steep on the right hand side, it's cut into those rocks. It's just nothing but rocks there. And it is pretty steep on this side and narrow, but they have started to go around the other way and then go on up, that also was steep, but a car would make it if the car was good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've got afour wheel drive, let's go for it. Want to drive up there now?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think we could get there now, because I don't think that that's open.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's give it a shot and see how close we can get so we know where it's going.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You can get, I think you can get to this Matthews place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: J.	Schneider's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who's homestead did you say this was, you said this was Junk Matthews' homestead here? I thought we just visited his homestead on the other side? Wasn't that Matthews' place we visited right before the. .

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had two places.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. That makes sense.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had two places, and the one house that he had here was right on that pinnacle up

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So right on the pinnacle in front of us along this old road bed here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what that old road is there, but that's where the road would have gone if I would have continued to own that place up there, I would have put the road right up this canyon.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see.

entries.speaker: A
