entries.text: I wouldn't have climbed this knoll here, you know, and then climb and then go clear up there and get on the level and then go back down a little bit to go into that draw up there where the house is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But his house was right up here on the pinnacle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let's see, I'm not sure we're looking at the right. . . same place here. From all the building they have there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's something up there, I could see it. There's something up there on that pinnacle, I don't know if it a house or what. . . it looks like a house to me, but. I don't know, there is a lot.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was Junk Matthews' homestead and one of the families would sta-y out here or one would stay out at his other place there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He had only one family.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The Schneiders.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These two families that I was telling you about, they were people that he had brought in here. Schneider was the name of one of them. But I can't remember the name of this other one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But the Schneiders would like live here and he'd live out at the other place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Schneiders lived right there in that house .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, on the pinnacle?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there another house right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then Junk Matthews lived on the other side of the stream?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He lived over yonder, yeah. He lived over in that house as long as they . . . as

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Schneiders lived here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so you'd go past the Schneiders on the way to and from school evety day.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I went right by them all the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Let's say right behind us where his horses bolted [we had just passed the area where Cook had found Matthews' body], was that crossing a creek or a gate down there? It's probably worth mentioning that Mary Bowman just said your house blew over in 1977, and she's the person living here now, so that would be over fifteen years ago, so that sounds about right. Can you think of anything else to add here? Do you know about how many trees were in that orchard? Just roughly.
bracketed_corrections: [we had just passed the area where Cook had found Matthews' body]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Our orchard up there?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was probably five apple trees, there were three cherry trees. And there was a walnut tree, that didn't grow very fast. That was about all, there was a. . . good gravenstein tree, and an apple bracket, but there's one. . . of the cherries, there's one Royal Anne, one Black Republican, and a pie cherry tree.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did Longfellow have any orchards beyond there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: On the Longfellow place?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a gravenstein tree there, and there was several other apple trees there, but the fir had grown up and choked a lot of the others, but the gravenstein tree was up where there wasn't anything else took over. It stayed there quite a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then on the Longfellow place, how far beyond your place was it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, our line fence . . . western line fence joined that place and I would say a mile between our house and where the buildings had been. There was a building there yet, a house, about a mile apart.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But nobody was living at the Longfellow place when you grew up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that was an old place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was an old place and they had a log cabin there that had rotted down, but there was a house there that was still all right to live in, the door was locked, but that

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: didn't stay locked too long. Somebody breaks the lock, you know, and then everybody could come or go, rats would go in there. Coons.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So yours was the only place between the Schneiders and Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, when Schneiders lived here, they didn't live here very long.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so when they did live here, yours was the only place between here and Kings Valley?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so there'd only be the two orchards and the one orchard was pretty well eaten by fir trees; it might have a gravenstein left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The one orchard on the Longfellow place?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The other apple trees below there, fir trees had choked them out, they didn't amount to anything, but there was a big silver maple.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they plant it? They must have.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have had to. It started to sprout, there was oodles and oodles of silver maples out from it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there's be silver maple and gravenstein to look for in that area.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think probably that the fir trees had crowded the silver maple out by now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That [road] goes up to the Pete Frank place. There used to be a place there a fellow by the name of Pete Frank that had a place there, but he left it. And it became a timber claim, Southern Pacific.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So on Pete Frank's place any old houses or orchards or anything associated with that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nothing but a big house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: A big house.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was just a big house, and my mother told me that he carried that lumber in there on his back to built it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who built this house right here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Johan son.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Johanson?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Johan son.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you recall about when?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. About 1935, '36, somewhere along in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there. . . and he replaced the Matthews' house essentially.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The Matthews' house was torn down I think by then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any house in between?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay so this is an old house in itself then.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: K.	Matthews' Accident Scene

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is the boundary to this 160 acre Matthews' place. Right there. That's the boundary.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now the boundaty here has got a little creek here, was this creek always through here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And this is where the horses started bolting on. . . you were telling us on Matthews?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, but they went out this way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, where did they find him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'm not too sure, but that. . . bog . . . I have looked and it ain't there anymore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: So I'm not sure, it ain't very far out to where that was and all of those poles that they put across, of course, were taken out of there. But this is where they got started. And down there after they hit that and it threw him out, why it wasn't very far until they got separated somehow, they probably one went on one side of the tree and the other one on the other side and broke the neck yoke and got rid of the tongue and there they split up so that they weren't even fastened together by the lines anymore, but they came down and Cook saw it and he realized that there was something wrong and he come on up here and found that old fellow stuck in that mire with his neck broke.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When was that about, what year was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I haven't got anything that I can trace it with. Wanda could probably tell you, because her husband found him.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so that would be before 1926, she moved out of here in 1926.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So Wanda's husband was the one that found him. Okay. Charlie that's probably the bog down in there, I'm guessing, this is the road going up to Baker Mountain, you were describing. You said this road went up and you had dOerent ways you could go out around here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How did those routes go from this road? We have Starker's gate up here off to our left which would be the north was this the way. . . did this road kind ofjust angle off up in here like this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know a thing about that road because that wasn't there. That is a logging road that has been put there recently. If she told you anything about this, why she probably knows, but I don't know a thing about this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think this is where when we were coming up you said, that the road went off and around Baker Mountain up in here about this point, was it down there further.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [ANGELA] There was no road, Bob, that's JU51 the route they went to school. Oh, it was just a trail?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, you mean when . . . that we walked?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This is where we started. This is where we started to go up but we went up by this right like that you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Straight up? So this was just a short cut to school from here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, I misunderstood, I thought it was a road.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No!

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you following any trail or anything or just making your own on it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We made a trail by walking it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. Okay. At this point here where we've got logging bridge down to our right and Starker gate to our left, and we're facing east this is the short cut over to the school.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Supposedly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Supposedly it was, but I don't remember now who it was that stood down below here and saw us going across there and told us later on that he believed that it would be

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: shorter to go around it on account of all these little dips. Now there's canyons coming down in there and we would go down where the sheep would have made trail, you know, instead of going down and up they'd angle here and then angle back again. So it made quite a loop to go right across it, it would be pretty steep, but he said that if we would go higher and get away from those or go lower down and get away from them, but we didn't do that we stayed on the trail. There were sheep trails, you know. And that was the way we went to school, we either went that way or we went this way or we went around Bakers Mountain from the other side and came on around Bakers Mountain and in from the right across from the school you could see Bakers Mountain, you know, if you go to the right of it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got one more question on that, those draws you were going up and down, would those draws have Doug fir in them? Or was that all bare in through those areas?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: These little gorges here?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were no trees. There were no trees there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, it was all pasture?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: L.	Cook's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're at the Cook house right here, first question is: Have you ever heard any stories about this house being haunted?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got stories now, three or four of them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, well, that . . . I wouldn't pay any attention to that, I think that .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I don't pay attention to them except that I keep hearing them diferent places. Now this is the Cook house and their ranch extended all the way up to your properly, except for Matthews?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Matthews was the only one in between us.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and this is where Wanda Cook and her husband and his uncle lived?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Cook's uncle?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I never knew him. That must have been after we . . . after I moved out of here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, the. . . she can tell me all about these orchards and that, can you recall anything through this area of particular. . . any particular memoiy of this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now you said that her husband was the one that found Junk Matthews and that they didn't have . . . they had two boys but they were a lot younger than you.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who had two boys?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Wan4a Cook.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She didn't have any kids, I don't think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She had two boys but they were a lot younger than you, so young you didn't even know about

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: them.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She could have had a family but I never knew it because after she married Cook and started to live here, you know, and I grew up and left the area, I didn't know what happened to her.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who lived here before the Cooks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nobody.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Nobody lived here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Nobody lived here before, he built this house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know who owned this land before the Cooks?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Baker.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, this is Baker's property. Where did the Bakers live?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just a little farther on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that would be Bakers Mountain right there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know the name of that hill over there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's still Bakers Mountain.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I mean the one. . . you can't see it probably. So from this point until Baker's place can you think of anything in between that's worth stopping at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, where's Baker's house was, we should probably stop and see if we can make

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: out where this place is here that you have a picture of.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I definitely want to stop at Baker's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I can't . . . from the picture, I can't tell for sure what was there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, okay, that's at Baker's. That's an old logging camp.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know where that is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're about ready to go.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: M.	Grabe's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're right here by Lorna Grabe's driveway. Where was Baker's from here? Baker's house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You're not to it yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We're not to it yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you seeing something over here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was nothing over there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was just all open pasture land. This orchard up to

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This house wasn't here either.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This little orchard to our right, it may have been Baker's orchard, that would have been before Cook's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's possible that Baker's made that, I don't remember seeing that. I kind of believe that it was planted afterwards . . . after I was out of here. Because if there had been anything there that would have had apples, we would had stopped and eaten some of them at times.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's why we've got you in the truck here.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: N.	Baker's House

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now, in this draw right here, this is Hosteter's house, where did they live at from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They had a big grape vine right up there. And as far as orchard is concerned I don't think they had any in here. Back in here was their barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, where this house is now about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Their house was right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Right on this knoll?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was right there, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, what happened to the Baker's house after Cooks bought it, did they tear it down or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was already down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know the Bakers?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, Baker was the girl that told me what "became" was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: 1Wat did she say it was?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The woman that wrote this thing . . . wrote that other book up. Got all that mixed up. Right in the back there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Marlene McDonald.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. I quote from her only because she's got some nice pictures in there. Eveiybody I've talked to said there are real problems with it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was . . . a man teacher, Mr. Wing, he lived in Corvallis, he walked over the ridge. He walked right over the ridge, over the Vineyard Mountain and over to the school house. And my folks taught us the Swedish language before they taught the American language, otherwise we would never have learned it. And when we had learned so that they figured that we should start to learn the American language they started to speak the American language. And when we started to school, Mr. Wing, had me come up and recite and I went up there and I read what I was supposed to read, you know, and I came to a word and I called it "become." And he stopped me, and he says "That isn't become." And I studied at it and studied at it and he didn't say anything and pretty quick he just grabbed me the neck and throwed me across his knee and gave me a darn good paddling. And sent me back to my seat and he said, "You study your lesson." And I went back to my seat. And after awhile he hollered down there and wondered, "Well, do you know what that is yet?" And I said, "No." Well, Verna Baker was sitting right back of me and she was about thirteen years old at that time and she watched him and when he wasn't looking she whispered in my ear, "became." I had called it "become." I didn't know there was such a thing as became.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he gave you a spanking for that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. So when he hollered the next time, and asked me, I told him "became." I

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: didn't know there was such a word as that, you know. A kid's vocabulary when he is six years old when he hasn't had but probably a year learning the American language became and become wouldn't be very much a part, you know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it common for those teacher to give spankings in those days?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, not too often.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did you think of Wing? Did you ever like him after that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, I didn't. And there were several older boys there, you know, that hadn't gone to school early enough so but what they were still in these lower grades when they were about nineteen, there was one of them that was in his twenties. And they certainly didn't have much faith in that Mr. Wing. I'm going to have to straighten her [Marlene McDonald] out because . . . if I get an opportunity because she has written that it was a woman teacher that give me a licking and that teacher, I fell in love with that teacher.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She got the wrong teacher.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She had the wrong one, she had Mr. Wing, honorable teacher and this woman supposed to given me a licking.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When you said [previous conversation] I had some mistakes in that book, I was glad it was some body else's reference.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway this teacher gave me her picture when school was out, she gave me her picture and it had a little string around the book that the picture was in and her picture and a little tassel on a string, you know, all pretty. If there were more teacher like that today, there would be a better world.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So she got the bad rap. . . she was the one that was blamed as the bad teacher by that other book. She was actually your favorite teacher.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was my favorite teacher, all right because she taught us a lot of things that wasn't in the book.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, you've got the record straight now.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She . . . one of those was, first of all, "to thine own self be true", "thou canst not then be false to any man". "Love without respect is an angel with but one wing".

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Love without respect is an angel with but one wing". Then there was another one

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: that was a song. "There's danger in flowing bowl, touch not, taste not, handle not; twil ruin body, ruin soul, touch not, taste not, handle not; twil lead the young and strong and brave, twil lead them to a drunkard's grave; twil lead them where no arm can save; touch not, taste not, handle not."

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Is that about alcohol?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Have you ever drank alcohol?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. What I have tasted in all my life wouldn't make you drunk if you drank it all at once.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, you did take it to heart.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'll tell you something that helped that. There was a family by the name of Swansons that lived just about three miles north of Corvallis and they came over on the same ship that my folks came over on. It was different times but they came from the same area. And we got acquainted with them, or my folks got acquainted with them. They had a big family and a big house. And we had Christmas dinner with them. And there was a little glass about so tall, [indicates 3 inches] by each plate. They had to have it formal just like they had it in Sweden, you know, everything had to be just right. We came to the table and I sat down where they put me and my folks were over on the other side of the table, my father and mother. And the first thing was somebody said grace. And next thing we pick up this little glass and touch it to our neighbor's glass and touch it the other neighbor's glass and then we would say "Skoll." And then we would take a sip and we'd put it back down again. And then we'd start passing the grub. Well, there was one glass that stayed there. Didn't get picked up and everything came to a dead stop, you know. I knew that every eye was on me, but I didn't flinch I just sat there. And I looked across and saw my father and mother but I didn't let them see that I saw them but they weren't embarrassed. They seemed to have a sort of a proud look. That helped me just as much as that little teacher that helped me because they didn't . . . I knew that they didn't . . . they weren't embarrassed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: They approved of your health and decisions over traditions.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: After I had sat there and just nothing happened for a little while, they all went ahead.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And when the dinner was over that glass sat right there yet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How old were you at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was seven.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: O.	DLC Survey Marker

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We're looking at a driveway here that goes to a new brown house, we just passed the R.K. Jones mailbox.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a big rock, there was a big boulder right off there and inscription on it as if it was a marker.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anything about it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That . . . yeah. I'm not sure, but what that is it right there, but it seems to me it was over farther. And for several years there was something there that had a cover over it. But this here had been a marker . . . a line. And that was to determine the line between the Baker place and this other place here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, this was the old survey marker then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That was the old survey marker.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's supposed to be, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and where's that located about?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, since this road has come down here now, I believe that doesn't belong where that marker was . . . I think it was right back yonder.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: By this little fir here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just on the other side of this fence row. This fence row is supposed to be the line. And that was intended to be from a survey way back, but somebody arranged to have another survey and I don't know who it was. Whether it was on this side or on that side. When they surveyed it again, the line was down here a quite a little ways probably about where you see those stakes down there coming up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You think the original survey was right here at the.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the original survey, but this . .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's to the left of the driveway here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: This later one . . . this driveway wasn't here. And all these houses wasn't here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But if this was the original donation land claim survey, they would have put the driveway down here following that survey line, that would have been if they built it a hundred years later. That's why I'm wondering which side of this driveway the stone was on.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anyway they went to court, and the court decided that the survey at that time . the present survey was the right line, so it moved the property line over. And this over here, they won much more land from down yonder and up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who owned the other land on the other side over there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dorgan.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Dorgan?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dorgan, I could name you about several of them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was just kind of curious who. . . this was the Baker place and I was wondering what the next place was called.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: If we go back, it would be Moore.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, the Moore place. Okay, so now we're heading into the Moore's place.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would be Moore and it would be Smith and it would be Lacy and

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We'll keep going that way, I don't want to get ahead of us, I just want to keep stopping at these places and identifying who was there and. . . we've gone by the Baker's place and the cooks bought from the Bakers and I've got Cook's up until 1926, so now we're heading over to the Moore place here. Is that correct?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: P.	Soap Creek Schoolhouse

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just passed Writsman's Creek Road. Was the Moore's house. . . where was the Moore's house from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You mean the owners . . . the original owners?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's a hump over yonder. There's a road that started in

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: is this the road we just passed here, somebody just came out of?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, that's . . . Dorgan house. That's the Dorgan house, it was built, but. .

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The blue house is the Dorgan house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He just built that, he married a woman that was a music teacher, he got acquainted with . . . they were Catholics, and he got acquainted with her in Portland. And then they got married, and she came out here. And there was something in France, so she could go back and get that she hadn't gotten when she was teaching there and she went back there. She couldn't stay because if there was something in the world that she didn't have in the way of music she was going to get it, but she went back there and then she came back here again and there was nothing here that they could teach her because she knew already and she was good. She could argue with you on something and then play a tune. She could sing one song and play another one. She knew how to put emphasis on a melody that we would just not put any emphasis on at all and wear it out. And she could put emphasis on that and hold and make it a beautiful melody.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What time was this that you heard her play?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What time?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, 1920's?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was probably in the fourth grade at that time, so

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, if I started at six and four that would be '10.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So,.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. We're getting my age in and the date wrong.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: You were born in 1898. I mean. . . 1910, I'm just trying to get to the nearest ten years.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When I was six years old, you know, why we'd have to take two years off on that other date because I wouldn't be six years old in 1906.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah, I'm just trying to get to the nearest ten years, I just wanted to know whether she played music in 1930's or 1920's or 1910. So I wasn't trying to get the exact year, but. So they lived here in 1908, in 1908 you could hear. . . she played music and she'd been to France. When did they build this house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: They . . . I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you know anything about anybody that was living up this draw?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There wasn't anybody living up in that draw. The stream that we got water from

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: came right down . . . we're just about sitting where it run across the road.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, that's the stream you're saying used to have fish? That's the stream that's on. that's the stream that's on page 26 here going on the guide [Soap Creek Auto Tour]. This building here I believe was up here about a quarter mile and there used to be a stream coming down by the school here and there used to be fish in that stream?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't think there was fish in it, there could probably be some up here a little ways, but you know, there was a fall in here just a little ways above where we got our water. We got out water for that school house right here, but there was a water fall that was probably four feet.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Four foot waterfall?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that was right up this draw here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was right up this draw.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What happened to the water here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, didn't happened anything to the water, the water was good.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where's the good water now, is what I mean?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, yeah, that's an indication again of what I told you about . . . I think we had 200 inches of rain fall at that time, when we haven't now got more than about probably 40 inches.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember about when this dried up?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It didn't just dry up suddenly.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you remember the last time it ran?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was still there when we were in the ninth grade, it was still there and it was good. I built a little water wheel on that water fall.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it dried up while you were a young man, stopped running when you were a young man?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I can't tell you just when it dried up because I wasn't here when it dried up.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was still running when you left here then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. And it was running across . . . there was a bridge here. There was a bridge and we had to cross three planks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was the school located in the same spot when you were a kid?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was located in that same spot, and when they cut that school house in two

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: and moved it across here and took it down to Tampico and put it back together again. Zorenson built that and we tried to get the date when that was built, but there was another way . . . I talked to this guy that was a rattle brain. Old, I don't know how old he was. But he didn't know where he had met me, but when I found out he lived in Philomath, I know that he hadn't met me probably but he knew that I had a school bus business there and he knew who I was, but I didn't know him. But after I got rid of him on the phone and was talking to Audrey, why we realized that he probably just knew me because I had a school bus business there. But he didn't know anything about this date. But we can get that date. We can get that date, I think.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'll tell you what happened. Angela was helping me work on this [Soap Creek Valley Auto Tour, Bob Zybach, OSU Research Forests cc: 1989] and we're putting it together and right about ten o'clock [p.m.] I got a call from Lorna Grabe just around the corner and she changed all this information from what I had written, but she knew these dates for sure. She said that this was constructed in 1932, and the previous school was constructed in 1899, and then I got this. . . there was a picture of another building here that she said was completed the previous year, but she said this school here was 1932.
bracketed_corrections: [Soap Creek Valley Auto Tour, Bob Zybach, OSU Research Forests cc: 1989]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, that is possible, but we can get that exact because they have records in there when the school started. And the other school had been missing for quite a while when this one was built and her records, all the records in there would give you the exact time when that school was started again.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And that's the woman that call me up and gave me those numbers there so it's not the same as that book that we've been referring to, but these numbers here. . . they were given to me the night before this went to press. So as near as I can tell, that's where the numbers are coming from, those have got to be the right numbers. But you went to school here about 1904 or 1905, something like that?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And so it was the building before this building?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it was the old. It was the building I went to school in was this big building that is shown here [in the Tour Book]. I don't know what page it's on, but there's a big building and it shows. My fingers are like sticks.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I didn't think I had any other school buildings in there, I think that was the only school

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: building they had, that one we were looking at there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, there is a point there that these people are probably a little touchy on, they would like to have that school the original school but it isn't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No that's 1932. I think we were just looking at the picture of the. . . I think that's the one you're looking for right there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, it is.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's 1899. Does that sound right, about the year after you were born?.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Just about.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you hear of any school being there before that building?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So even this building wasn't. . . it shows. . . there's a picture, there's a building I cut off of this to fit the page here, there's a picture right here and they said that was built in 1898 just the year before.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: The picture that's on the wall up there, that I spoke to you about this morning, the picture of that will show you the original school house which is then on that picture the wood shed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got that picture. It shows some people standing in front of it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I think you might even be one of the people.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. There's that great big tall Miss Dullen, seven footer I believe.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was really that tall? Or she just looked that way?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, she was immense. You can tell by the picture you know compared with the other people.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But on that picture, you said you have it already.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: You can see the original school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She was saying the original school was only built a year before that school, the wood shed school they said they just built for temporary use before the next school went in.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well that one that . . . the wood shed on that picture was the school for quite a while.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: She said just one year, and before that I thought it was back to the 1870's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who said that?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Loma Grabe.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She wasn't born when that took place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No. Neither were you if it was 1870's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But my brother went to school and his picture is on that. He is ten years older than I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: He was going to that school ten years before this one was built.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay that's.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He's holding something that he had gotten from the teacher, I don't know what it is, it couldn't have been a certificate. . . I don't know what it was. Award of Honor or something. And Moore is on that picture.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Gan. . . you went to school here, you walked here, we can see Bakers Mountain there and we've covered the routes you've covered on it and you've said these people here, you can't remember when they built their house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would . . . I hate to guess at it. That's what I'm pert near apt to do.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Did they live in a house before this house? Because she was playing music about 1908, this house. . . does it look like.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Dorgan himself lived here, he was single, he lived back there on that hill, you can't see it now from this shed, but there's a hill over there and there was a house on top of it and that whole works before that lived in that house and this one wasn't here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay that house. . . can we back up and look at that. That house back there where Dorgan lived then, that's the one I'm interested in. That's where he got that house from the people before him. That was the old house. Okay. That's the Alfred Writsman's homestead. That's what we've been tiying

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's no house there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah. Where would that be from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there's another house built there now.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: [ANGELA] Do you want to drive down there? Yeah, let's do that.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Q.	Zeolite Hills Road

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: All of this here has been ruined according to what it was then. It had been ruined by making this road. Because that was just a smooth knoll.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: This was a smooth knoll here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was just a smooth knoll and there was a house setting right on top of it right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We've come up that Moss Rock Drive and we're taking Zeolite Hills Road and this knoll to our left with these oaks on it, that was the original homesite.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know of any Indian arttfacts or anything in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Any what?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Any Indian artifacts?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Most of these old cabins were built on old Indian sites. But this. . . was it a log house here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, it was a large farmhouse built of lumber. I played for that. . . for a dance right there one night and when it was over they came out with a lantern you know to see me off, there was a picket fence around it. And I got onto my bicycle and I had my fiddle in one of those plastic cases, had a strap over and it was on my back. And I started to coast down that hill, now there's a road that went this way across right at the bottom and there was a blacksmith's shop.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, you know where the blacksmith's shop is?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I know where it was.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Good let's head for it.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It [the road] would go over between the blacksmith's shop and a barn.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And what was that barn, was that the barn that went to this house here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That barn went to that house up there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What did they call this house, was this the Moore house?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's the house that Moores were in. But they didn't call it that, because there was so many, there was probably seven people that lived in that house and owned this place.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it the Modie house? Or Modic?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Who?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Modie, or Modic?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Modie never had it. I never knew a Modie.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, he was here in the 1840's. I don't know why he left.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was out of here in 1940.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, oh.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I'm tiying to go back to some of this stuff This house up here was an old donation land claim. And so it was before Moores and this was the road coming through and it hit the old road that you said went down the valley here, went down this side of the creek, is that correct?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, I would tell you if you would let me.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But the road came down from that hill and right at the bottom of that hill it could go around the black smith's shop and leave the black smith's shop on the right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Back there then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, you go around that black smith shop and leave it on the right and on the other side was a barn. I go through between the black smith's shop and the barn and come over on one road and go down here or I could right between that same barn that I just spoke about and another big barn on the other side. And go right down another road and come together down here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So there were two roads that came out.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There were two roads that came out here, one was on that side of this little stream, that was a pretty good sized creek in those days, one on that side and one on this

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: side. But they came together down here in order to cross the main creek over the bridge.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So back there on the knoll was the old house. if we're looking backwards where the black smith shop from right here, where would that have been? There's two barns and a black smith's shop, is that correct?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where would the black smith's shop have been from here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's pretty hard to tell.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: But we went around it, and had it on our right.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: R.	Govier's Sawmill

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're by Alvie Govier's place right here. A yellow house and where was the sawmill located from here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Right straight up from the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Straight behind?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, right up straight from the house about fifty yards.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Now, Goviers still live there don't they, some members of the Govier family.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know any Goviers alive now that would know about that sawmill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Jup.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jup?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Alvie Govier's boy would know. We tried to call him. This guy in Philomath that couldn't tell where he met me, he gave us a phone number and he said it was Jup and in Salem.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Jupiter?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I don't know what his real name was, they always called him Jup.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Then Audrey called that number and they didn't know anything about any Goviers. So this rattle brain you know . . . he got the wrong number.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, so do you know when Alvie Govier built that house there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Alvie Govier built that house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know about when?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It would have to be about the time that he got married, he married Neva Nebon, from the east and they came out here . . . it would have to be . . . pert near have to get something I can associate with it, you know, it's pretty hard to just pin point a date.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I was just curious about when, it doesn't matter exactly, do you know about when their mill got started, was their mill going when you were a boy?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was going to school, I was pretty well along in school when he married that. . . he had a little idea that probably he would marry my sister when she got old enough. I was trying to figure out about some date and he was a pretty nice guy, respectable sort of a guy, but this Neva Nebon grabbed him. And Hilda was probably about fifteen years old at that time, and I would be thirteen and a half.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So, she was how much younger than you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: A year and a half older.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So it would have been about 1915, he got married, and then he built the house about the time he got married.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When did he start the mill?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Pretty quick after that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So right around World War I, he started the miii?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was there any other mill going in this valley then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So that would have been the only mill going at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know of any mill between Sulphur Springs mill that we already looked at and this mill, any other mill going at that time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was one back of the school house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was one back there, but I was so little at that time, that I can't even tell you if I was two years old or if I was three years old or if I was only one year old. But we

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: went down there and there was somebody that had an accident some way and they had operated on him, I think he had lost an arm or something and they had operated on him, but he was under ether at the time and they would call his name once in a while and he'd grunt. But they were trying to bring him to. That was a sawmill there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: About the turn of the century then?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was it operating?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was operating at that time because he had that accident you know. And they had a sawdust pile that we kids could go back and play on when we went to school.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But it wasn't operating while you were growing up, it was a real old sawmill.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was gone. It was gone when I started to go to school, why it was gone.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did you have any name associated with it or anything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So we had the Govier sawmill, Sulphur Springs sawmill, and then a third saw,nill site in back of the school that was there before the turn of the century. On the Goviers, I'm going to be talking to somebody else about their family history so I can get some information from them. Can you think of any other thing associated with this site that you might think is important or interesting?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: S.	Lee Brown's Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Lee Brown's place had silver maple, is that maybe what some of these things that have gone to weed here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think there's still sprouts from that silver maple.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now Lee Brown was one Brown brother that hadn't murdered anybody.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And you worked with him?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So the Browns lived down through this area about the turn of the century, and towards the Tampico area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, I know the name of the family that lived here in the 1930's, but we didn't know the older family. Do you know where Lee Brown moved after this?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he died here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, because this is a prime prospect for excavation.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a family that moved in here and the house burned. And I think the whole family burned up except for one.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: The dad and the boy lived.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah. The dad came home and it was a fire and he went in and got the boy out, carried him out. But I think it burned the rest of them. I don't remember the name. It seems like it was Etridge. [}{ildebrandt]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I've got the name, I talked with Gene Glender and he knew all about this, so we're getting into an area where I've got a good histoiy on it, back there you're the only history we've got, so. . . okay.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: T.	The Marcks' Place

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, we're at the Marc/cs house now, Marcks built this house, didn't he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: These people here think this house was built in 1850.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Goviers built a barn for Marcks right over here and a little wind blew it down.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We just passed the old teacher cottage there, where your sister used to come and stay with Mrs. Harris and Miss Allen.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Did they ever use that cottage as a school site? Did they ever teach classes out of there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. Oh, no.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, and this is the Marc/cs house here. Okay. And can you think of anything about this house in particular?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: There used to be a barn across the road that blew down and. . . I've got one more question, there's a real old apple orchard out across the Soap Creek on the road. . . on Tampico Road, do you know anything about any old apple orchards or anything in this area?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No. No, I wasn't familiar with that area. We came home from the hop yard and Goviers came out and talked to us and they needed another hand and I was about thirteen years old and my father didn't figure that I should go down there but they out ruled him you know and I kind of wanted to, so I went down there the next morning and I pitched for them for. . . only about two weeks left of threshing. That was my first year out and my first time out to work out. I developed younger than most people and when I was thirteen or fifteen I was as big as I ever got.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Let me ask you one or two quick questions about why your family came here, we're just about out of tape. They came here from Sweden right?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you tell me what year and how they came the United States?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was a lot of immigrants that came across on the Lusitania from the old country and the desire to get to some place where they could get land, that was it, and my father left you know and came over here and he started in the east and there was nobody that wanted to hire anybody, they all wanted to get land. He kept coming farther and farther west and when he got to Tigard, Tigardville, he got to Tigardville, it's part of Portland now. But it was a separate town then, there he got his first real job and it was a dollar a day.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know what year that was that he came out here?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I could trace things back a while and I could get it . . . but, you know, I wasn't born yet when that happened.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Your brother was born about 1888.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was ten years older than I.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your dad and mom were probably married 1887?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Somewhere along in there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And he'd been in the United States for how many years?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, my brother, I think, was ten years old when or nine years old before my father had enough money so that he could send for the two of them. But he got his first job at Tigardville, a dollar a day, ten hour day. And then he moved from there to Corvallis and he started to work for Fisher's Feed Mill, Fisher's Flour Mill. And there his wages were a little higher and he continued to stay with that until he got

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: enough money so that he could send for them.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Where were they at?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: In Sweden.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your brother was born in Sweden?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So your dad came out here after 1888? Your dad got married in Sweden, he already had a family when he left there.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah, he had to buy two tickets, you know to come out here, to bring his family out here.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I see. I misunderstood. He came out by himself, I thought he was a single man. He was married and with a family. What town were they from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Calsang.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Calsang, Sweden.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your family has been there for a long time?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's one of them. One of them was from Calsang and the other one was from Frieda.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Freida? And that was your mother?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No, my mother was from Calsang.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay, what was her maiden name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Anna Frestrom.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Frestrom? Okay, so your dad was married there and then he came out here and he worked in corvallis, saved enough money, sent for them, and so about that time must have been when he purchased this land.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We worked that flour mill until he had enough money so that he could buy a little something somewhere and he had $400 when he went out on Soap Creek and bought a guy's right that had started to homestead this place that we had. He could have bought about four acres of land right in Corvallis at that same time with that $400, about four acres, but they didn't realize what things was going to be, you know, what things was going to do and he wanted to get out some place where he was free and that was it. He was free there and we could run stock, we had lots of cattle and they

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: could run clear to Kings Valley, clear to Airlie and clear almost to Corvallis and Soap Creek was the shortest distance they could come four miles was about all they could come if they came in this direction. But

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Who did he buy the claim from?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think his name was Sather or Sether or something like that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can you. . . I've got a pretty clear idea now. . . we've covered all the time from when you were born until you left here and then some after and some before. Can you think of any think else about the histoty of this valley that we haven't maybe discussed or that you think is important? Have we covered about everything?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's nothing that I can think about is important to this, it would be important to me of course but not in this.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Something that's important to you that you think might be important to use here.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, the thing that's important to me was when the Armistice was signed.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: Part II.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: June 16, 1990 Interview

entries.speaker: editorial
entries.text: The second interview with Charlie Olson took place in his home, near Summit in Lincoln County, Oregon on June 16, 1990. We started the interview by examining two photos from his family album; a family portrait taken a little after the turn of the century, and a photo of his sister in front of the family Soap Creek homestead following a snow storm a few years before World War I.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 1.	Family Homestead

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Whenever you are ready to go Charlie we can

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Start on any of them, and I should have made a little sketch of what I should say and what I should report on but I haven't.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There's so many things that it would take quite a lot of literature to copy it all down and read it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Before we talk about the armistice, if you want I could make a little list and then go back to the list.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It doesn't make any difference as long this will report when, and a fellow can go on up to a certain point and take something else, another topic, and can bring it up to that point if a fellow can remember it and do it.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Yep. Well that's why I've got an index in this. So we can skip around and then we can come right back and somebody reading the index can put it together. But I do know we want to talk about the Armistice and your personal experiences and want to talk about family life and home life, how your mom did the washing, what you ate, how you put up food, djfferent times of the year, that type of thing if we could.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, it don't matter to me which day we start.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: We looked at this picture right here. [Picture of Olson family, about 1901-1904.]

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [Mrs. Olson] Yeah, that's the family (Olson) right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Can I borrow these pictures and copy them at school?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [Mrs. Olson] Well, I think so.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Is that your mom and dad?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That's gotta be you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And your older brother and your sister.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And we've got all the names on the first recording so if I can copy this and then this is your homestead there. Is that your mother in front? [Second picture of Olson homestead in snow.]
bracketed_corrections: [Second picture of Olson homestead in snow.]

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's my sister right there. And that's the barn. This picture is correct. We have several that are not.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Do you know when this photograph was taken?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I'd have to figure a while before I could tell you that. My sister on there was probably about 16.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And she was born a year and half after you?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Before.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh, before you. So this would be maybe 1912?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That would be close enough.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: And then the barns in the background on the lefihand side with Bakers Mountain behind it, what's that building there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That building is not a building. You mean that white spot?

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: No, this building here, the large building.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was the house.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. And then this off to the side, is that a kitchen?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's an addition. That was a porch.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why is it enclosed like that? Was it used for storage?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was a built-in addition later on.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: So this is the home that your dad built after you were born.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I was born down here [indicates spot on picture] in a log cabin while he was building that right there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: And that roof stays on that. That's made out of the old yellow fir. That roof was

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: made out of shingles that he shaved out of what they called old growth then, yellow fir. And they stayed on that house until I think after you took a picture from the air, you told me you had a picture of it. I think the roof was still on it when that picture was taken. [Referring to 1948 aerial photographs.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. So this place was built what, about 1898?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He was building that right in 1898, yes, he was building it then.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Now that pipe coming out it looks like a metal pipe. Is that a metal pipe on the roof there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's a stove pipe. That stove pipe came from both stoves, the heater and stoves in what we call the other room, and then the kitchen, of course, they came together, and they went out in one stove pipe. Just the stove pipe, nothing else.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What would you use for firewood?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Wood, nothing but wood.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Would you use yellow fir or would you use oak?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: We used mostly willow and fir.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Why would you use willow? Just soft to cut, or.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There was no particular. We cut wood from many things. And there was no particular choice or any particular schedule on the wood that we used. We just burned wood, whatever wood we happened to get at that time. The woodshed is a little ways back of that house. It doesn't show it. It would be back here, back of Hilda's shoulder this way, a log cabin. That was put full of wood every summer, late summer, you know, fall, and used during the winter.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many cords would it hold?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was never measured, and it was never any uniform length. It was just whatever a fellow could cut it into and then haul it to the woodshed on the sled. And then bucksawed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh I see, so once you got it to the shed then you prepared it for the stove. What's that small building off to Hilda's ?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That was, on the side there, that held our milk and cream and butter; kind of a little cold storage. The sun didn't get on that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: That looks like it would be the east side.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: is that the north side?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It's on the north.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Well we're seeing Bakers Mountain here which would be to the south. Oh I see, it would be kind of northeast, almost. Were you ever at the old homestead?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [MRS. OLSON] Oh yes, all the time.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Oh. Were the parents still living there then?

entries.speaker: narrator-2
entries.text: [MRS. OLSON] The father was there, and his stepmother.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How long did your father live there? When did he finally move out?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: He moved out from Corvallis just about a year before I was born. He was working for the mill. Fisher's Mill. Flour.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Then how long did he stay?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Well, he moved out just a short time before I was born.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: I mean, how long did he stay at this homestead then? How long did he live there?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: That's a little difficult to get. We got him, we moved him out here [Summit] when he got too old. My stepmother has a little deed to the place. That she would stay with him up there until the last. And that got so hard to get to, muddy or slick. Probably three miles of nothing but dirt road and [unintelligible]. And I bought a little house for him right over here at the Y [Summit intersection between Blodgett, Eddyville and Hoskins], and moved him out here. And this stepmother had a will that if she stayed with him until the last she could have the whole thing. And when we moved him out here, she began to get scared that he would change that will. He wouldn't have done it of course. But I bought that house over here on the Y at the corner and I deeded that to her. And he didn't think I should, he thought I should have deeded it to myself, but I deeded it to her and told him that the reason was that if he had an automobile accident, he was still driving, that he wouldn't lose his home. And that seemed to satisfy him. So that was hers over there too, but she was terribly scared that he would change that will, just scared to death.
bracketed_corrections: [Summit intersection between Blodgett, Eddyville and Hoskins]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was she a pretty nice lady that you were concerned about that? Your stepmother, was your stepmother a pretty nice person?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She was, in a certain way, yes. But a neighbor woman over here knew her brother in New York, and my stepmother wanted to go to New York and see him, and I loaned

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: her the money, my father wouldn't give her the money, I loaned her the money. I gave her the money I should say, so that she could go over there and visit her brother. He told . . . Ms. Smith, she was married . . . and he told her that it's no use, any amount of money she get ahold of, she will spend it, that is my stepmother would, she would spend it on an airplane ticket from here to Sweden and back. And that kind of loused things up a little bit, but I never told her that we knew that her brother had said that, and she, this neighbor woman, also told us that he kicked his sister out of there.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: In New York.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: What was your stepmother's name?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hannah.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Okay. Your sister's name is Hannah too isn't it?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Hilda.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Hilda. Okay, that's what I was getting confused. How long after your father died did your stepmother continue to live at the homestead?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: She never did live there after he died. We moved them away from there. I don't mean never, I mean after we brought them out here, she didn't go back up there. But there is a lawyer in Portland by the name of Gitner that had gotten a three-year option on that home, that Soap Creek home, a three-year option to take the timber off for $3,000. Timber wasn't worth anything in those days. That three-year option was seventeen years old when we went in to the lawyers I was doing my business with to have this timber cut on that home and by a fellow by the name of John Weinert. And he was going to take a section and pay a downpayment what they figured that one section of, not a regular section but a marked off square, and he would pay down on that approximately, and then when that was taken off they would adjust one way or the other and they'd mark off another square. And when we came in there to have this settlement drawn up, Gitner, the lawyer from Portland was there with my lawyers. I can't think of their names, there was three of them. Anyway, they started in to bother my father, he was there, and they put him clear at the other end of the room, and then they were in the middle and then they put me clear over here at the

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: other end. And when they started to make a deal with him, I realized that they was gonna try to install in his mind that they still had this option. So I spoke up pretty loud, and said "If he decides to sell it to you, would you be willing to pay more than that obsolete option?" [It was only a 3-year option.] And he said "Yes." But my father missed it, I know that he missed it. And they started to bother him to make a price. And after a while why they decided, well make a price on the whole thing, not just the timber but the whole thing, the land. What went through my mind at the time, I should have probably done it but I didn't, if I'd got up and go around there and take him out of there and tell him "let's get out of here before they want you to pay them something so they can have the whole thing." But I didn't do it because there was that one thing her brother had told this woman "everything that she gets she'll spend it on airplane tickets between Sweden and here." So I just sat quiet and let him take it. He made them a price and then they took it right now, I don't remember what the price was for sure.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: How many acres was

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It was 160 acres.

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: It was 160, and in 1914, the [Benton] County cruised that to 15 million board feet. That 15 million board feet was yellow fir. And in the meantime, from 1915 until somewhere around 1955 or something, I'm only guessing, there had been a lot of this second growth. So there was a lot of timber on there. [C.O. Addendum: Timber cruising by the Forestry people then was as far off as it is yet at times 3 times too little or 3 times too much.]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Forty years of growth. What year did your father sell the lanil?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: What year did he sell it? He sold it right then. And I don't remember the year. I'd have to guess and I could probably miss it quite a little bit. [Maybe 1950]

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: It's not too important. Did your stepmother take the money and go to Sweden like her brother said?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Apparently. Apparently she did. [Not until my father died.] And I don't know how long it took her to get rid of it. And then she began to find out that it was worth a whole lot more than she got, and she came back and tried to get them to, out of just

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: sympathy, you know, give her approximately what it would be worth or quite a lot more, but of course they wouldn't do that. So she went back to Sweden and married a man back there just to get the citizenship paper so that she could be taken care of there in her old age. They were socialistic, Sweden was a social government, and they would take care of the older people in probably a better form than they do here now. We haven't caught up with the world on that.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Was your father a socialist?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Oh yeah. Everybody in Sweden were socialistic. They were a socialist country.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Were you a socialist?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Me? It has taken me about 78 years to decide what I am. I have been on the fence. I registered as an independent so that I could vote independently, but I soon learned that that deprived me of everything, only just certain things. Then I continued to stay that way, and I have stayed that way, until -- I am still registered that way.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Independent?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: Independent.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: But have you ever decided whether you are a socialist or not?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: There is no difference between socialism, democracy and communism. There's three Constitutions. The Constitution of those three, socialism, democracy and communism, they mean exactly the same thing, they cover the same thing. So I am still registered as an Independent. But I would go democratic if we had a democracy. But we haven't got it. We haven't got a democratic system and we never have had. It is nothing but a bureaucratic [system}. And it constantly becomes more and more and more bureaus. And if anybody can gain a position where he could start to make it democratic they'll kill him. Lincoln was the first one that they killed.

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: Well, he was registered Republican wasn't he?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: I think he was. But I don't know -- the histories, I've been told it's airight, but I lost faith in the histories after I saw that quite a lot of history and then read what it was supposed to be afterwards. I never would sit down and swallow the history after I began to learn what they did.

entries.speaker: heading
entries.text: 2.	World War I

entries.speaker: Q
entries.text: When World War I came up, at that time your family was socialist. What did your parents feel about you maybe having to go to war?

entries.speaker: A
entries.text: When they ran in the paper that this student army training corps [S.A.T.C.] was ready to be shipped, they were at the door, and a sergeant came and told me, it was during noon while we were eating, and I went to the door and talked to them and I didn't tell them what I knew was coming. Of course, they came down and said goodbye. But I didn't tell them the situation because it would have worried them quite a lot. We had soldiers and there was no corporals. They just gave the order on this line, fall in, count off, and right dress. One two three four, one two three four, one two three four. Every number one man was a corporal. And when they yelled, right front in to line, that corporal would take his squad and get them in the right position, and right front and on front that would be from a different situation to form a different line. But that guy, whoever it happened to be, the number one man, he would have to take his squad to a new position. We would do everything that they could yell at us, and we carried Enfields [rifles]. And not one word had they given us the entire time on the nomenclature of those guns. They didn't tell us what caliber it was even. And I had started when I was quite a kid to work with guns, and I knew quite a little bit about it. But the kids as a rule, you know, didn't know how to take the safety off or put it on.
